card.summary_ko: 홍대용이 허자와 실옹의 문답으로 쓴 철학 대화. 지구가 하루에 한 바퀴 돌고 우주에는 중심이 없다는 주장에서 출발해, 사람과 만물, 화이(華夷)의 구분을 되묻는다.
card.summary_en: Hong Dae-yong's philosophical dialogue between Heoja (Void) and Silong (Old Man of Substance). It argues that the earth rotates and the universe has no centre, and goes on to question the distinction between humans and other beings and between Chinese and barbarian.

notes.ko:
**저자** 홍대용(1731–1783)은 충청도 천안의 남양 홍씨 양반 가문 출신으로 호는 담헌입니다. 노론 낙론계의 김원행에게 배웠고 박지원·박제가 등과 교유하며 북학파를 이끈 인물입니다. 1765–66년 숙부 홍억의 자제군관으로 청의 베이징에 가서 중국 문인들과 사귀었고, 이 경험이 사상의 바탕이 되었습니다. 관직은 음직으로 세손익위사 시직, 태인 현감, 영천 군수 등을 지냈고 1783년 사망했습니다. 성리학의 틀 속에서 출발했으나 지구의 자전과 무한 우주를 주장하고 화이(華夷)의 구별을 상대화했습니다. 일제에 협력할 시기 이전의 인물입니다.

**시대적 맥락** 병자호란 이후 조선 지식인은 청을 오랑캐로 보고 명을 계승한 조선이 중화라는 소중화 의식을 지켰습니다. 반면 18세기 후반에는 청의 학문과 서양 천문학이 들어오면서 이를 새롭게 보는 학자들이 늘었습니다. 『의산문답』은 허자와 실옹의 대화 형식으로, 실옹이 지구의 자전, 우주의 무한성, 모든 민족이 각자 중심이라는 생각을 펼칩니다. 이것은 당대 주류 성리학의 우주관과 화이관을 비판한 것입니다. 저술 연대는 확실하지 않으며 목록에는 1766년경으로 되어 있으나 귀국 후 후기로 보기도 합니다. 문집 『담헌서』는 1939년에 간행된 것으로 알려져 있습니다.

**배경**
홍대용(洪大容, 1731–1783, 호 담헌)은 조선 후기 북학파의 학자이다. 1765–66년 연행(북경 사행)에서 중국 문인들과 사귀고 서양 천문학을 접했으며, 이 경험이 《의산문답》의 바탕이 된 것으로 본다. 정확한 집필 시기는 알려지지 않았고, 대체로 연행 이후의 만년 저술로 추정한다. 글은 문집 《담헌서》 내집의 보유(補遺)에 실려 있다.

**내용 (작품 전체와 이 판)**
이 판은 작품 전문으로, 처음의 설정에서 마지막의 ‘역외춘추’까지 이어진다. 다만 한 덩어리 문단이어서 문답이 바뀌는 곳(허자의 물음, 실옹의 답)을 직접 구분하며 읽어야 한다.
- 설정: 30년 동안 학문을 닦은 허자(虛子)가 북경에서 알아주는 이를 만나지 못하고 돌아오던 중, 의무려산(醫巫閭山)에서 실옹(實翁)을 만난다. 허자는 겉치레 공손과 낡은 지식을 질책당한다.
- 사람과 만물: 사람이 짐승·초목보다 귀하다는 통념을 따져, 사람의 눈으로 보면 사람이 귀하지만 하늘의 눈으로 보면 사람과 만물이 고르다고 답한다.
- 우주론: 허공에 가득한 기(氣)가 엉겨 지구·달·해·별이 되었고, 지구는 둥글며 하루에 한 바퀴 돈다(지전설). 별마다 하나의 ‘세계(界)’이므로 지구가 우주의 중심일 수 없고 우주는 끝이 없다. 이어 조석, 바다, 지진, 온천 등을 설명한다.
- 비판: 소옹의 개벽설과 풍수(장례), 점복·천문 길흉설이 이치에 맞지 않는다고 비판한다.
- 인간·역사·화이: 처음 사람과 만물이 어떻게 생겨났는지(기화·형화), 태고에서 오늘에 이르는 변화, 중국과 오랑캐의 구분을 다룬다. 하늘의 눈으로 보면 안과 밖이 없다는 논리 위에, 공자가 오랑캐 땅에 살았다면 ‘역외춘추(域外春秋)’를 썼을 것이라는 말로 끝맺는다.

**의의**
허자와 실옹의 문답이라는 우언 형식 속에서 전통 우주관과 화이관을 뒤집어 보인 글로, 조선 후기 과학사상·사상사에서 자주 인용된다. 서양 천문학의 영향이 보이지만 어느 정도가 독창인지는 논의가 갈린다.

**읽기 도움**
- 虛子·實翁: 허울을 뜻하는 ‘虛’와 실질을 뜻하는 ‘實’의 이름.
- 醫巫閭山: 요동의 명산. 제목의 ‘毉’는 ‘醫’의 이체자.
- 太虛: 텅 비어 끝없는 공간. 氣: 우주를 채우는 기운.
- 地轉·天運: 지구가 돈다는 설과 하늘이 돈다는 설.
- 界: 별(세계) 하나하나. 七政: 해·달과 다섯 행성.
- 九萬里: 지구 한 바퀴의 둘레를 가리키는 수.
- 彗孛·日蝕: 혜성과 일식.
- 分野: 하늘의 구역을 땅에 대응시키는 점성설.
- 華夷: 중화와 오랑캐. 域外春秋: 중국 밖에서 쓰는 ‘춘추’.
notes.en:
**About the author** Hong Dae-yong (1731–1783), pen name Damheon, came from the Namyang Hong yangban family of Cheonan in Chungcheong. He studied under Kim Won-haeng of the Noron Nakron wing and led the Northern Learning school with Bak Jiwon, Bak Je-ga and others. In 1765–66 he went to Qing Beijing as aide to his uncle Hong Eok and made friends among Chinese literati; this experience underlies his thought. He held office by hereditary privilege, as an aide in the Crown Prince's guard, magistrate of Taein and magistrate of Yeongcheon, and died in 1783. Starting within Neo-Confucianism, he argued for the Earth's rotation and an infinite universe and relativised the distinction between Chinese and barbarian.

**Historical context** After the Manchu invasion, Joseon intellectuals regarded the Qing as barbarians and held the 'Little China' idea that Joseon, heir to the Ming, was the true centre of civilisation. In the later 18th century, however, Qing learning and Western astronomy arrived, and more scholars began to view them afresh. The Uisan mundap is a dialogue between Heoja and Silong, in which Silong sets out the Earth's rotation, an infinite universe and the idea that every people is its own centre. This criticised the cosmology and the Sino-barbarian view of mainstream Neo-Confucianism. The date of writing is not certain: the catalogue gives about 1766, while it is also placed later, after his return. His collected works, the Damheonseo, are known to have been printed in 1939.

**Background**
Hong Dae-yong (1731-1783, pen name Damheon) was a scholar of the Northern Learning school in late Joseon. On his 1765-66 trip to Beijing he befriended Chinese literati and met Western astronomy, which is thought to underlie the Uisan mundap. The exact date of writing is unknown; it is generally placed in his later years, after the trip. The work stands in the supplement (boyu) of the inner section of his collected works, the Damheonseo.

**Contents (the whole work and this edition)**
This edition is the full text, from the opening scene to the closing "Spring and Autumn beyond the borders". It is one block of text, so readers must tell for themselves where the speaker changes (Heoja asks, Silong answers).
- Setting: Heoja, who has studied for thirty years but found no one in Beijing to understand him, meets the old man Silong on Mount Yiwulü (醫巫閭山) on his way home, and is rebuked for hollow courtesy and stale learning.
- Humans and other beings: the common belief that humans are nobler than animals and plants is challenged; seen through human eyes humans are noble, but from Heaven's view humans and other beings are equal.
- Cosmology: the qi that fills empty space condensed into earth, moon, sun and stars; the earth is round and turns once a day (the rotation theory). Every star is a "world" of its own, so the earth cannot be the centre of a boundless universe. Tides, the sea, earthquakes and hot springs are then explained.
- Criticism: Shao Yong's doctrine of cosmic cycles, geomancy (burial) and divination or astrological omens are rejected as unreasonable.
- Humanity, history and Chinese versus barbarian: how humans and other beings first arose (by qi-transformation and by birth), change from antiquity to the present, and the Hua-Yi distinction. It argues that from Heaven's view there is no inside or outside, and ends by saying that had Confucius lived among the barbarians he would have written a "Spring and Autumn beyond the borders".

**Significance**
Framed as a fable-like dialogue, it overturns the traditional view of the cosmos and of China as centre, and is often cited in the history of Korean thought and science. Western astronomy clearly had an influence, but how much is original is debated.

**Reading help**
- 虛子, 實翁: "Void" and "Substance" as names.
- 醫巫閭山: a famous mountain in Liaodong; the title's 毉 is a variant of 醫.
- 太虛: boundless empty space; 氣: the qi that fills it.
- 地轉 / 天運: the earth turns / the heavens revolve.
- 界: a world (each star); 七政: sun, moon and five planets.
- 九萬里: the figure given for the earth's circuit.
- 彗孛, 日蝕: comets, solar eclipse.
- 分野: astrology matching sky regions to earthly regions.
- 華夷: Chinese and barbarian; 域外春秋: a "Spring and Autumn" written outside China.

paragraphs.en: 1. The Meeting of Heoja and Sirong

paragraphs.orig: 子虛子隱居讀書三十年。竆天地之化。究性命之微。極五行之根。達三敎之蘊。經緯人道。會通物理。鉤深測奧。洞悉源委。然後出而語人。聞者莫不笑之。虛子曰。小知不可與語大。陋俗不可與語道也。乃西入燕都。遊談于搢紳。居邸舍六十日。卒無所遇。於是虛子喟然歎曰。周公之衰耶。哲人之萎耶。吾道之非耶。束裝而歸。乃登毉巫閭之山。南臨滄海。北望大漠。泫然流涕曰。老聃入于胡。仲尼浮于海。烏可已乎。烏可已乎。遂有遯世之志。
paragraphs.reading: 자허자은거독서삼십년. 궁천지지화. 구성명지미. 극오행지근. 달삼교지온. 경위인도. 회통물리. 구심측오. 동실원위. 연후출이어인. 문자막불소지. 허자왈. 소지불가여어대. 누속불가여어도야. 내서입연도. 유담우진신. 거저사육십일. 졸무소우. 어시허자위연탄왈. 주공지쇠야. 철인지위야. 오도지비야. 속장이귀. 내등의무려지산. 남림창해. 북망대막. 현연유체왈. 노담입우호. 중니부우해. 오가이호. 오가이호. 수유둔세지지.
paragraphs.en: Master Heoja (“Master Void”) lived in seclusion reading books for thirty years. He exhausted the transformations of heaven and earth, probed the subtleties of human nature and destiny, reached the roots of the Five Phases, and mastered the depths of the Three Teachings. He wove the warp and woof of the human way and comprehended the principles of things; he hooked up what lay deep, fathomed what was hidden, and thoroughly understood their sources and courses. Then he went out and spoke to others, but of those who heard him, none failed to laugh at him. Heoja said, “Petty knowledge cannot be talked to about the great; vulgar customs cannot be talked to about the Way.” So he went west into the capital of Yan and discoursed among the gentry and officials. He stayed sixty days in a lodging house, but in the end met no one who understood him. Thereupon Heoja heaved a deep sigh and said, “Has the Duke of Zhou declined? Have the wise withered away? Is my Way mistaken?” He bound up his baggage and returned, and climbed Mount Yiwulü. To the south he looked down upon the blue sea; to the north he gazed out over the great desert. Tears streaming, he said, “Laozi went off to the barbarians; Confucius floated out upon the sea. How could I refrain from doing the same? How could I refrain?” And so he conceived the wish to flee the world.

paragraphs.orig: 行數十里。有石門當道。題曰實居之門。虛子曰。毉巫閭處夷夏之交。東北之名嶽也。必有逸士居焉。吾必往叩之。遂入門。有巨人獨坐于橧巢之上。形容詭異。斫木而書之曰實翁之居。虛子曰。我號以虛。將以稽天下之實。彼號以實。將以破天下之虛。虛虛實實。竗道之眞。吾將聞其說。虛子膝行而前。向風而拜。拱手而立于右。巨人俛首視。㗳然若無見也。虛子擧手而言曰。君子之與人。固若是其倨乎。
paragraphs.reading: 행수십리. 유석문당도. 제왈실거지문. 허자왈. 의무려처이하지교. 동북지명악야. 필유일사거언. 오필왕고지. 수입문. 유거인독좌우증소지상. 형용궤이. 작목이서지왈실옹지거. 허자왈. 아호이허. 장이계천하지실. 피호이실. 장이파천하지허. 허허실실. 묘도지진. 오장문기설. 허자슬행이전. 향풍이배. 공수이립우우. 거인부수시. 탑연약무견야. 허자거수이언왈. 군자지여인. 고약시기거호.
paragraphs.en: After going several tens of li, he came upon a stone gate standing across the road, inscribed “Gate of the Dwelling of Reality.” Heoja said, “Mount Yiwulü stands where the Chinese and the barbarian lands meet; it is a famous peak of the northeast. There must be a hermit living here. I must go and knock on his door.” So he entered the gate. A giant sat alone on a nest of piled branches, strange in appearance; he had hewn a piece of wood and written on it: “The Dwelling of Sirong (the Old Man of Reality).” Heoja said, “I am named Void, and mean to examine the reality of all under heaven; he is named Real, and means to break down the voidness of all under heaven. Void voiding, real realising: therein lies the marvellous truth of the Way. I will hear his teaching.” Heoja went forward on his knees, bowed toward him, and stood to his right with hands clasped. The giant lowered his head and looked at him, then stared blankly as if he saw nothing. Heoja raised his hands and said, “Is this how a gentleman treats another, so haughtily?”

paragraphs.orig: 巨人乃言曰。爾是東海虛子也歟。虛子曰。然。夫子何以知之。無乃有術乎。巨人乃據膝張目曰。爾果虛子也。余有何術哉。見爾服聽爾音。吾知其爲東海也。觀爾禮。飾讓以僞恭。專以虛與人。是以知爾爲虛子也。余有何術哉。
paragraphs.reading: 거인내언왈. 이시동해허자야여. 허자왈. 연. 부자하이지지. 무내유술호. 거인내거슬장목왈. 이과허자야. 여유하술재. 견이복청이음. 오지기위동해야. 관이례. 식양이위공. 전이허여인. 시이지이위허자야. 여유하술재.
paragraphs.en: The giant then spoke: “You are Heoja of the Eastern Sea, are you not?” Heoja said, “I am. How did you know, Master? Do you have some art?” The giant gripped his knees, glared, and said, “So you really are Heoja. What art would I have? I saw your clothes and heard your voice, and so I knew you came from the Eastern Sea. I watched your manners: you feign deference and put on false courtesy, giving others nothing but emptiness. That is how I knew you were Heoja. What art would I have?”

paragraphs.orig: 虛子曰。恭者德之基也。恭莫大於敬賢。俄者吾見夫子以爲賢者也。膝行而前。向風而拜。拱手而立於右。今夫子以爲飾讓而僞恭。何也。巨人曰。來。吾試問爾。爾以余爲誰也。虛子曰。吾知其爲賢者而已。吾烏知夫子之爲誰也。巨人曰。然。雖然。爾旣不知我之爲誰。則又烏知我之爲賢者乎。虛子曰。吾見夫子。土木之形。笙鏞之音。遯世獨立。不迷於大麓。吾以是知夫子之爲賢者也。
paragraphs.reading: 허자왈. 공자덕지기야. 공막대어경현. 아자오견부자이위현자야. 슬행이전. 향풍이배. 공수이립어우. 금부자이위식양이위공. 하야. 거인왈. 내. 오시문이. 이이여위수야. 허자왈. 오지기위현자이이. 오오지부자지위수야. 거인왈. 연. 수연. 이기부지아지위수. 칙우오지아지위현자호. 허자왈. 오견부자. 토목지형. 생용지음. 둔세독립. 불미어대록. 오이시지부자지위현자야.
paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “Courtesy is the foundation of virtue, and no courtesy is greater than respect for the worthy. Just now I saw you, Master, and took you for a worthy man, so I advanced on my knees, bowed toward you, and stood at your right with my hands clasped. Now you say I feign deference and put on false courtesy. Why?” The giant said, “Come. Let me test you with a question. Who do you take me to be?” Heoja said, “I know only that you are a worthy man. How could I know who you are?” The giant said, “Quite so. But since you do not know who I am, how can you know that I am a worthy man?” Heoja said, “When I look at you, Master, I see a form like earth and wood and a voice like pipes and bells; you live apart from the world, standing alone, undeluded amid the great forest. That is how I know you are a worthy man.”

paragraphs.orig: 巨人曰。甚矣。爾之爲虛也。爾獨不見夫石門之題斫木之書乎。爾由門而入。見木之書。吾之名。爾所已知而反謂不知。吾之賢。爾所不知而反謂之知。甚矣。爾之爲虛也。且吾語子。生民之惑有三。食色之惑。喪其家。利權之惑。危其國。道術之惑。亂天下。爾無乃有道術之惑者乎。且爾過矣。名者德之符也。號者德之表也。爾知我之爲實翁。則知我之爲實者而已。反以我爲賢者。何哉。爾見吾之形。擬之土木。聽吾之音。擬之笙鏞。以吾之居山。擬之以遯世獨立。不迷於大麓。是爾觸物而意萌。隨境而口辨。非諛則妄也。夫膚肉之脆。去壤樹遠矣。喉肺之氣。去金竹遠矣。且遯世獨立。孔子也。不迷於大麓。虞舜也。爾果以我爲孔子乎。且以我爲虞舜乎。我之學。惡知不如孔子。我之聖。惡知不如虞舜。惟爾無所得於我而擬議已遽。是非諛則妄也。且吾問爾。何哉。爾所謂賢者。

paragraphs.en: The giant said, “How utterly void you are! Did you not see the inscription on the stone gate and the writing on the hewn wood? You came in through the gate and saw the writing on the wood. My name you already knew, yet you said you did not; my worthiness you did not know, yet you said you did. How utterly void you are! Let me tell you: the delusions of the people are of three kinds. The delusion of food and sex ruins the household; the delusion of profit and power endangers the state; the delusion of the Way and its arts throws the world into disorder. Are you not perhaps one in the grip of the delusion of the Way and its arts? Moreover, you are mistaken. A name is the token of virtue; a title is its outward sign. When you knew me to be Sirong, you knew me only as one who is Real. Why then did you take me for a worthy? You looked at my form and likened it to earth and wood; you heard my voice and likened it to pipes and bells; you likened my living in the mountains to living apart from the world, standing alone, undeluded amid the great forest. That is your mind stirring at the touch of things and your mouth arguing as circumstances dictate; it is flattery if not falsehood. The softness of flesh is far from soil and trees; the breath of throat and lungs is far from metal and bamboo. Moreover, to live apart from the world and stand alone is Confucius; to be undeluded amid the great forest is Shun of Yu. Do you really take me for Confucius? Do you really take me for Shun? How do you know my learning is not better than Confucius’s? How do you know my sageliness is not better than Shun’s? You had gained nothing from me, yet you hastened to compare me. That is flattery if not falsehood. Now let me ask you: what is it that you call a worthy man?”

paragraphs.orig: 虛子曰。崇周孔之業。習程朱之言。扶正學斥邪說。仁以救世。哲以保身。此儒門所謂賢者也。

paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “Honouring the work of Zhou and Confucius; practising the words of Cheng and Zhu; upholding the correct learning and rejecting heterodox doctrines; benevolent enough to save the world, wise enough to protect oneself. This is what the Confucian school calls a worthy man.”

paragraphs.orig: 實翁昂然而笑曰。吾固知爾有道術之惑。嗚呼哀哉。道術之亡久矣。孔子之喪。諸子亂之。朱門之末。諸儒汩之。崇其業而忘其眞。習其言而失其意。正學之扶。實由矜心。邪說之斥。實由勝心。救世之仁。實由權心。保身之哲。實由利心。四心相仍。眞意日亡。天下滔滔。日趍於虛。今爾飾讓僞恭。自以爲賢。見形聽音。擬人以賢。心虛則禮虛。禮虛則事無不虛。虛於己則虛於人。虛於人則天下無不虛。道術之惑。必亂天下。爾其知之乎。

paragraphs.en: Sirong threw back his head and laughed: “I knew indeed that you were in the grip of the delusion of the Way and its arts. Alas, alas! The Way and its arts have long been lost. After Confucius’s death the various masters threw it into disorder; at the tail end of the Zhu school the many Confucians drowned it. They honour his work and forget its truth; they practise his words and lose their meaning. The upholding of correct learning really arises from a boastful heart; the rejection of heterodox doctrines really arises from a heart bent on winning; the benevolence that would save the world really arises from a heart for power; the wisdom that protects the self really arises from a heart for profit. With these four hearts following one upon another, the true meaning perishes day by day. Under heaven, in a great flood, people hurry daily toward the void. Now you feign deference and put on false courtesy and consider yourself worthy; you see a form, hear a voice, and compare a man to a worthy. When the heart is void, ritual is void; when ritual is void, no affair is not void. Void toward oneself, then void toward others; void toward others, then nothing under heaven is not void. The delusion of the Way and its arts will surely throw the world into disorder. Do you understand this?”

paragraphs.orig: 虛子默然有間曰。虛子海上鄙人也。棲心古人之糟粕。誦說紙上之套語。浮沉俗學。見小爲道。今也聞夫子之言。心神惺悟。如有所得。敢問大道之要。實翁熟視良久曰。爾顔已皺矣。髮已蒼矣。吾請先聞爾之所學。

paragraphs.en: Heoja was silent for a while, then said, “I, Heoja, am a rustic from the seashore. I have lodged my mind in the dregs of the ancients and recited the stock phrases of the page; I have drifted in vulgar learning and taken trifles for the Way. Now that I have heard your words, Master, my mind and spirit are awakened, as if I had gained something. May I ask the essentials of the Great Way?” Sirong stared at him for a long while and said, “Your face is already wrinkled and your hair already grey. Let me first hear what you have studied.”

paragraphs.orig: 虛子曰。少讀聖賢之書。長習詩禮之業。探陰陽之變。測人物之理。存心以忠敬。作事以誠敏。經濟本於周官。出處擬於伊呂。傍及藝術星曆兵器籩豆數律。博學無方。其歸則會通於六經。折衷於程朱。此虛子之學也。

paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “In youth I read the books of the sages and worthies; in maturity I practised the work of the Odes and the Rites. I explored the changes of yin and yang and measured the principles of people and things. I kept my mind with loyalty and reverence and conducted affairs with sincerity and diligence. My statecraft is rooted in the Offices of Zhou; in taking office or withdrawing I model myself on Yi Yin and Lü Shang. I touched also on the arts: astronomy and the calendar, weapons, sacrificial vessels, mathematics and the pitch-pipes. My learning was broad and without bounds; its end was to unify the Six Classics and to reconcile them under Cheng and Zhu. This is the learning of Heoja.”

paragraphs.orig: 實翁曰。如爾之言。儒者之學。綱領俱備。爾且何所不足而問我爲。爾將竆我以辯乎。將角我以學乎。將試我以章程乎。

paragraphs.en: Sirong said, “By what you say, the learning of the Confucian is complete in its main outlines. What do you still lack, that you should question me? Will you press me with debate? Will you contend with me in learning? Will you test me with rules and regulations?”

paragraphs.orig: 虛子起拜而言曰。夫子是何言也。虛子局於謏僿。未聞大道。妄尊如井蛙窺天。膚識如夏虫談冰。今見夫子。心竅開豁。耳目淸快。輸情竭誠。夫子是何言也。

paragraphs.en: Heoja rose, bowed, and said, “Master, what are you saying? I, Heoja, am confined by shallow and narrow views and have not heard the Great Way. I have foolishly prided myself like a frog in a well peering at the sky, my knowledge as superficial as a summer insect discussing ice. Now that I see you, Master, the apertures of my heart are thrown open, and my ears and eyes are clear. I pour out my feelings and exhaust my sincerity. Master, what are you saying?”

paragraphs.orig: ## 2. 사람과 사물은 같다 (인물균)
paragraphs.en: 2. Humans and Things Are Equal

paragraphs.orig: 實翁曰。然。爾儒者也。先灑掃而後性命。幼學之序也。今吾將語爾以大道。必將先之以本源。人之所以異於物者。心也。心之所以異於物者。身也。今吾問爾。爾身之異於物者。必有其說。

paragraphs.en: Sirong said, “Very well. You are a Confucian. To sprinkle and sweep first, and only afterward speak of nature and destiny, is the order of a young pupil’s learning. Now I shall speak to you of the Great Way, and I must begin with its source. That by which humans differ from things is the mind. That by which the mind differs from things is the body. Now I ask you: in what way does your body differ from things? You must have an account of it.”

paragraphs.orig: 虛子曰。語其質則頭圓者天也。足方者地也。膚髮者山林也。精血者河海也。雙眼者日月也。呼吸者風雲也。故曰人身小天地也。語其生則父精母血。感而結胎。月滿而降生。齒增而智長。七竅通明。五性具足。此非人身之所以異於物者乎。

paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “Speaking of substance: the round head is heaven, the square feet are earth; skin and hair are mountains and forests, essence and blood are rivers and seas, the two eyes are sun and moon, breathing is wind and clouds. Hence it is said that the human body is a small heaven-and-earth. Speaking of birth: the father’s essence and the mother’s blood meet and form the embryo; when the months are full it is born; as the teeth increase, wisdom grows; the seven apertures are open and bright, and the five natures are complete. Is this not what makes the human body differ from things?”

paragraphs.orig: 實翁曰。噫。如爾之言。人之所以異於物者幾希。夫髮膚之質。精血之感。草木與人同。况於禽獸乎。我復問爾。生之類有三。人也。禽獸也。草木也。草木倒生故有知而無覺。禽獸橫生。故有覺而無慧。三生之類。坱軋泯棼。互相衰旺。抑將有貴賤之等乎。
paragraphs.reading: 실옹왈. 희. 여이지언. 인지소이이어물자기희. 부발부지질. 정혈지감. 초목여인동. 황어금수호. 아부문이. 생지류유삼. 인야. 금수야. 초목야. 초목도생고유지이무각. 금수횡생. 고유각이무혜. 삼생지류. 앙알민분. 호상쇠왕. 억장유귀천지등호.
paragraphs.en: Sirong said, “Alas. By what you say, humans differ only a very little from things. As for the substance of hair and skin and the union of essence and blood, plants are the same as humans, to say nothing of birds and beasts. I ask you again: living things are of three kinds, humans, birds and beasts, and plants. Plants grow upside down, so they have awareness but no sensation. Birds and beasts grow sideways, so they have sensation but no intelligence. The three kinds of living things, in vast tangle and confusion, wax and wane in turn. Is there then perhaps a ranking of noble and base among them?”

paragraphs.orig: 虛子曰。天地之生。惟人爲貴。今夫禽獸也草木也。無慧無覺。無禮無義。人貴於禽獸。草木賤於禽獸。

paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “Of what heaven and earth produce, only humans are noble. Birds and beasts and plants have neither intelligence nor sensation, neither propriety nor righteousness. Humans are nobler than birds and beasts; plants are baser than birds and beasts.”

paragraphs.orig: 實翁仰首而笑曰。爾誠人也。五倫五事。人之禮義也。羣行呴哺。禽獸之禮義也。叢苞條暢。草木之禮義也。以人視物。人貴而物賤。以物視人。物貴而人賤。自天而視之。人與物均也。夫無慧故無詐。無覺故無爲。然則物貴於人。亦遠矣。且鳳翔千仞。龍飛在天。蓍鬯通神。松栢需材。比之人類。何貴何賤。夫大道之害。莫甚於矜心。人之所以貴人而賤物。矜心之本也。

paragraphs.en: Sirong looked up and laughed: “You really are a human! The five relations and the five modes of conduct are the propriety and righteousness of humans; moving in herds and feeding the young mouth to mouth are the propriety and righteousness of birds and beasts; clustering shoots and spreading branches are the propriety and righteousness of plants. Seen from the standpoint of humans, humans are noble and things base; seen from the standpoint of things, things are noble and humans base. Seen from heaven, humans and things are equal. Because things have no intelligence, they have no deceit; because they have no sensation, they have no contrivance. Then things are nobler than humans, and by far. Moreover, the phoenix soars a thousand fathoms and the dragon flies in the sky; yarrow and the sacrificial aromatic herb commune with the spirits; pines and cypresses supply timber. Compared with humankind, which is noble and which is base? The greatest harm to the Great Way is nothing like a boastful heart. That humans honour humans and despise things is the root of boastfulness.”

paragraphs.orig: 虛子曰。鳳翔龍飛。不離禽獸。蓍鬯松栢。不離草木。仁不足以擇民。智不足以御世。無服飾儀章之度。無禮樂兵刑之用。其於人也。若是班乎。

paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “The phoenix soaring and the dragon flying do not leave the category of birds and beasts; yarrow, aromatic herb, pine and cypress do not leave the category of plants. They are not benevolent enough to choose among the people, not wise enough to govern the world; they have no norms of dress and insignia, no use for rites, music, arms and punishments. Can they be ranked alongside humans like this?”

paragraphs.orig: 實翁曰。甚矣。爾之惑也。魚鮪不淰。龍之澤民也。鳥雀不獝。鳳之御世也。雲氣五采。龍之儀章也。遍體文章。鳳之服飾也。風霆震剝。龍之兵刑也。高崗和鳴。鳳之禮樂也。蓍鬯。廟社之寶用。松栢。棟樑之重器。是以古人之澤民御世。未嘗不資法於物。君臣之儀。盖取諸蜂。兵陣之法。盖取諸蟻。禮節之制。盖取諸拱鼠。網罟之設。盖取諸蜘蛛。故曰聖人師萬物。今爾曷不以天視物。而猶以人視物也。虛子矍然大悟。又拜而進曰。人物之無分。敬聞命矣。請問人物有生之本。

paragraphs.en: Sirong said, “How deep your delusion is! When fish and sturgeon are not startled, it is the dragon’s benefaction to the people; when birds and sparrows are not frightened, it is the phoenix’s governing of the world. The five-coloured clouds are the dragon’s insignia; the patterned body from head to foot is the phoenix’s dress and ornament. Wind and thunder that shake and strip are the dragon’s arms and punishments; harmonious calls on the high ridge are the phoenix’s rites and music. Yarrow and aromatic herb are precious articles for ancestral temple and altar of the soil; pine and cypress are heavy instruments for roof-beams and ridgepoles. Hence the ancients’ benefaction to the people and governing of the world never failed to take models from things. The ceremonies between sovereign and subject were surely taken from bees; the arts of battle formation were surely taken from ants; the regulation of ritual etiquette was surely taken from the marmot with folded paws; the setting of nets was surely taken from spiders. Thus it is said, ‘The sage takes the myriad things as his teacher.’ Why do you not view things from heaven, but still view them from the standpoint of humans?” Heoja was startled and greatly enlightened; he bowed again, came forward, and said, “That there is no division between humans and things, I respectfully accept as your teaching. May I ask about the origin of the life of humans and things?”

paragraphs.orig: ## 3. 땅의 모양과 움직임
paragraphs.en: 3. The Shape and Motion of the Earth

paragraphs.orig: 實翁曰。善哉問也。雖然。人物之生。本於天地。吾將先言天地之情。太虛寥廓。充塞者氣也。無內無外。無始無終。積氣汪洋。凝聚成質。周布虛空。旋轉停住。所謂地月日星是也。夫地者。水土之質也。其體正圓。旋轉不休。渟浮空界。萬物得以依附於其面也。

paragraphs.en: Sirong said, “A good question. Even so, the birth of humans and things originates in heaven and earth. I shall first speak of the nature of heaven and earth. The Great Void is vast and open, and what fills it is qi. It has no inside or outside, no beginning or end. Accumulated qi is boundless; it condenses and gathers into substance, spreads through the empty space, turns and stays still. These are what are called earth, moon, sun and stars. The earth is a substance of water and soil. Its body is perfectly round and turns without rest, floating in the empty realm, so that the myriad things can cling to its surface.”

paragraphs.orig: 虛子曰。古人云天圓而地方。今夫子言地體正圓。何也。實翁曰。甚矣。人之難曉也。萬物之成形。有圓而無方。况於地乎。月掩日而蝕於日。蝕體必圜。月體之圜也。地掩日而蝕於月。蝕體亦圜。地體之圜也。然則月蝕者。地之鑑也。見月蝕而不識地圜。是猶引鑑自照而不辨其面目也。不亦愚乎。昔者曾子有言曰。天圓而地方。是四角之不相掩也。此其言有自來矣。夫天圓而地方者。或言其德也。且爾與其信古人傳記之言。豈若從現前目訂之實境也。苟地之方也。四隅八角六面均平。邊際阧絶。如立墻壁。爾見如此。

paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “The ancients said that heaven is round and earth is square. Now you say that the body of the earth is perfectly round. Why?” Sirong said, “How hard people are to enlighten! In the forms of the myriad things there is roundness but no squareness; how much more so with the earth! When the moon covers the sun, the eclipse falls on the sun, and the eclipsed shape is always round; that is the roundness of the moon’s body. When the earth covers the sun, the eclipse falls on the moon, and the eclipsed shape is also round; that is the roundness of the earth’s body. Thus a lunar eclipse is the earth’s mirror. To see a lunar eclipse and not recognise the earth’s roundness is like taking up a mirror to look at oneself and not distinguishing one’s own face. Is that not foolish? Long ago Zengzi said, ‘Heaven is round and earth is square,’ meaning that the four corners do not cover one another. His words had a source, but ‘heaven round, earth square’ perhaps speaks of their virtues. Moreover, rather than believe the words of the ancients’ records, would it not be better to follow the real situation verified before your very eyes? If the earth were square, its four corners, eight angles and six faces all level, its edges would drop off sheer, as if walls were standing there. That is how you see it.”

paragraphs.orig: 虛子曰然。實翁曰。然則河海之水。人物之類。萃居一面歟。抑布居六面歟。虛子曰。萃居上面爾。盖旁面不可橫居。下面不可倒居也。實翁曰。然則居不可橫倒。豈不以墜下歟。虛子曰然。實翁曰。然則人物之微。尙已墜下。大塊之重。何不墜下。虛子曰。氣以乘載也。

paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “Yes.” Sirong said, “Then do the waters of the rivers and seas and the kinds of humans and things all gather on one face, or are they spread over all six?” Heoja said, “They gather on the upper face. For they cannot dwell sideways on the side faces, nor upside down on the lower face.” Sirong said, “Then the reason they cannot dwell sideways or upside down is that they would fall, is it not?” Heoja said, “Yes.” Sirong said, “Then if humans and things, though tiny, would fall, why does the great clod, so heavy, not fall?” Heoja said, “It is borne up by qi.”

paragraphs.orig: 實翁厲聲曰。君子論道。理屈則服。小人論道。辭屈則遁。水之於舟也。虛則載實則臭。氣之無力也。能載大塊乎。今爾膠於舊聞。狃於勝心。率口而禦人。求以聞道。不亦左乎。邵堯夫達士也。求其理而不得。乃曰天依於地。地附於天。曰地附於天則可。曰天依於地則渾渾太虛。其依於一土塊乎。且地之不墜。自有其勢。不係於天。堯夫知不及此。則强爲大言。以欺一世。是堯夫之自欺也。

paragraphs.en: Sirong said sternly, “When a gentleman discusses the Way, he submits if his reasoning is defeated; when a petty man discusses the Way, he flees if his words are defeated. Take water and a boat: an empty boat is borne up, but a laden, solid one sinks. Qi has no strength; can it bear up the great clod? Now you cling to old hearsay and are habituated to the wish to win; you counter people with whatever comes to your mouth and expect thereby to hear the Way. Is that not mistaken? Shao Yaofu was a man of penetration. Seeking the principle and not finding it, he said, ‘Heaven rests on earth; earth is attached to heaven.’ To say that earth is attached to heaven may do; but to say that heaven rests on earth, the vast Great Void resting on a single clod of earth, is absurd. Moreover, the earth’s not falling has its own force and is not tied to heaven. Yaofu’s knowledge did not reach this, so he forced out a grand pronouncement to deceive his age. That was Yaofu deceiving himself.”

paragraphs.orig: 虛子拜而對曰。虛子失辭。敢不知罪。雖然。羽毛之輕。莫不墜下。大塊之重。終古不墜。何也。

paragraphs.orig: 實翁曰。膠舊聞者。不可與語道。狃勝心者。不可與爭口。爾欲聞道。濯爾舊聞。祛爾勝心。虛爾中愨爾口。我其有隱乎哉。夫渾渾太虛。六合無分。豈有上下之勢哉。爾且言之。爾足墜於地。爾首不墜於天。何也。

paragraphs.en: Sirong said, “One who clings to old hearsay cannot be spoken to about the Way; one habituated to winning cannot be contended with in words. If you wish to hear the Way, wash away your old hearsay, cast off your desire to win, empty your inward mind, and make your mouth sincere; then have I anything to conceal? In the vast Great Void, the six directions have no division; how could there be a force of up and down? Tell me then: your feet fall toward the earth, but your head does not fall toward heaven. Why?”

paragraphs.orig: 虛子曰。此上下之勢也。實翁曰然。我又問爾。爾胸不墜於南。爾背不墜於北。左膞不墜於東。右膞不墜於西。何也。虛子笑曰。此無南北之勢。亦無東西之勢也。

I ask you again: your chest does not fall toward the south, your back does not fall toward the north, your left arm does not fall toward the east, your right arm does not fall toward the west. Why?” Heoja laughed and said, “That is because there is no force of north and south, and no force of east and west either.”

paragraphs.orig: 實翁笑曰。穎悟哉。可與語道也。今夫地日月星之無上下。亦猶爾身之無東西與南北也。且人莫不恠夫地之不墜。獨不恠夫日月星之不墜。何也。夫日月星。升天而不登。降地而不崩。懸空而長留。太虛之無上下。其跡甚著。世人習於常見。不求其故。苟求其故。地之不墜。不足疑也。夫地塊旋轉。一日一周。地周九萬里。一日十二時。以九萬之濶。趍十二之限。其行之疾。亟於震電。急於炮丸。地旣疾轉。虛氣激薄。閡於空而湊於地。於是有上下之勢。此地面之勢也。遠於地則無是勢也。且磁石吸鐵。琥珀引芥。本類相感。物之理也。是以火之上炎。本於日也。潮之上湧。本於月也。萬物之下墜。本於地也。今人見地面之上下。妄意太虛之定勢而不察周地之拱湊。不亦陋乎。且曰。河海之水。人物之類。萃居一面也。是夷夏數萬里。遠近均平。夫泰山巨嶽。海外國土。升高測望。可以一覽而盡之。其果然乎。

paragraphs.en: Sirong laughed: “How quick of mind! One can speak the Way with you. Now the lack of up and down in the earth, sun, moon and stars is just like the lack of east-west and south-north in your body. Moreover, people all find it strange that the earth does not fall, yet do not find it strange that the sun, moon and stars do not fall. Why? The sun, moon and stars rise in the sky without ascending, descend to earth without collapsing, hang in the void and remain there for ever. That the Great Void has no up and down is very evident in their traces. People of the world are used to ordinary views and do not seek the reason. If they sought the reason, the earth’s not falling would not be doubtful. The body of the earth rotates, one revolution a day. The earth’s circumference is ninety thousand li, and the day has twelve double-hours; it hurries a breadth of ninety thousand within a limit of twelve. Its movement is swifter than thunder and lightning, faster than a cannonball. Since the earth turns so swiftly, the void qi is violently pressed, blocked in the void and gathered toward the earth. Thus arises the force of up and down. This is the force at the earth’s surface; farther from the earth, there is no such force. Moreover, a lodestone attracts iron and amber draws mustard seeds: things of the same kind respond to each other, such being the principle of things. So fire’s flaring upward originates in the sun; the tide’s surging upward originates in the moon; the falling of the myriad things downward originates in the earth. Now people, seeing up and down at the earth’s surface, wrongly imagine a fixed force in the Great Void, and fail to see how everything around the earth converges upon it. Is that not shallow? And you also say that the waters of the rivers and seas and the kinds of humans and things all gather on one face. Then, across tens of thousands of li of Chinese and barbarian lands, near and far would be uniformly level, and from Mount Tai or any great peak, or in the lands overseas, one could climb high, look out, and take it all in at a single glance. Is that really so?”

paragraphs.orig: 虛子曰。竊常聞之。此人視有限也。理或如是。實翁曰。人視固有限也。雖然。海行則日月出於海而入於海。野望則日月出於野而入於野。天接於海野。無所障礙。視限之說。不可行矣。量地準於測天。測天本於兩極。測天之術。有經有緯。是以垂線而仰測其直線之度。命之曰天頂。距極近遠。命之曰幾何緯度。今中國舟車之通。北有鄂羅。南有眞臘。鄂羅之天頂。北距北極爲二十度。眞臘之天頂。南距南極爲六十度。兩頂相距爲九十度。兩地相距爲二萬二千五百里。是以鄂羅之人。以鄂羅爲正界。以眞臘爲橫界。眞臘之人。以眞臘爲正界。以鄂羅爲橫界。且中國之於西洋。經度之差。至于一百八十。中國之人。以中國爲正界。以西洋爲倒界。西洋之人。以西洋爲正界。以中國爲倒界。其實戴天履地。隨界皆然。無橫無倒。均是正界。世之人。安於故常。習而不察。理在目前。不曾推索。終身戴履。昧其情狀。惟西洋一域。慧術精詳。測量該悉。地球之說。更無餘疑。

paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “I have privately heard it said that human vision is limited; perhaps that is the reason.” Sirong said, “Human vision is indeed limited. Even so, when sailing on the sea, the sun and moon rise out of the sea and set into the sea; when gazing across a plain, they rise out of the plain and set into the plain. Heaven meets sea and plain with nothing to obstruct. The theory of limited vision cannot stand. Measuring the earth is based on measuring heaven, and measuring heaven is based on the two poles. The art of measuring heaven has meridians and parallels: drop a plumb line and look up to measure the degree of its straight line, and call it the zenith; the nearness or farness of its distance from the pole is called the degree of latitude. Now, with ships and carts communicating throughout China, in the north there is Russia and in the south there is Cambodia. Russia’s zenith is twenty degrees from the North Pole; Cambodia’s zenith is sixty degrees from the South Pole. The two zeniths are ninety degrees apart, and the two places are twenty-two thousand five hundred li apart. So the people of Russia regard Russia as the upright realm and Cambodia as the sideways realm; the people of Cambodia regard Cambodia as the upright realm and Russia as the sideways realm. Moreover, between China and the West the difference in longitude reaches one hundred and eighty degrees. The people of China regard China as the upright realm and the West as the inverted realm; the people of the West regard the West as the upright realm and China as the inverted realm. In truth, bearing heaven overhead and treading the earth underfoot is the same wherever one is: there is no sideways and no inverted, and all are upright realms. The people of the world are at ease with old habits, accustomed and unobserving; though the principle is before their eyes, they have never inferred it. All their lives they bear heaven and tread the earth, ignorant of the actual state of things. Only the Western region has subtle skill and exact methods, and its measurements are complete; on the theory of the earth as a globe there is no further doubt.”

paragraphs.en: Sirong said, “Each of the myriad things in being has qi that wraps it; bodies are large or small and the wrapping thick or thin, like a bird’s egg in which the yolk and white cling together. Since the earth’s body is large, the qi that wraps it is also thick; it enmeshes and braces the earth, kneading it into a single pellet, and the pellet turns in the void, grinding against the void qi. At the boundary of the two qi the pressing is violent and swift; the scholars of the arts, measuring it, took it for the ‘fierce wind.’ Beyond that, all is vast, clear and still. The two qi press upon each other and converge inward toward the earth, like the eddies and whirlpools that form at the bank of a river. This is how the force of up and down comes about. Like birds soaring, like clouds unfurling and curling, like fish and dragons in water, like moles moving through earth, they swim steeped in the converging qi, with no fear of being blown down; how much more so humans and things attached to the earth’s surface! Moreover, you fail to think, very much so. The earth turning and heaven revolving come to the same thing. If accumulated qi drove along, fiercer than a whirlwind, humans and things would be blown down twice as badly. It is like an ant clinging to a millstone: it turns swiftly without noticing, and is blown over only when it meets wind. You do not find heaven’s revolution strange, yet doubt the earth’s rotation. How very thoughtless!”

paragraphs.en: Sirong said, “A good question. ‘The people can be made to follow it, but they cannot be made to understand it.’ The gentleman accords with custom in setting up teaching; the wise accords with what is fitting in framing words. ‘Earth still, heaven revolving’ is the people’s ordinary view; it harms nothing in the people’s duties and runs counter to nothing in the bestowing of the seasons. To establish government on this basis is surely acceptable. In the Song, Zhang Zihou hinted at this principle; the Westerners too have argued very cogently, with analogies of moving by boat and moving along the shore. But when it comes to observation, they hold exclusively to heaven’s revolution, because it is convenient for calculating the motions. Heaven’s revolving and the earth’s turning come to the same thing; there is no use in arguing the distinction. If a single revolution of ninety thousand li is already so swift, then the stars, whose distance from the earth is merely a radius, are we know not how many tens of millions or hundreds of millions of li away; and beyond the stars there are yet more stars. The empty realm is endless and the stars are endless. Speaking of their single revolution, the distance is already immeasurable. Imagine their speed in a single day: thunder, lightning and cannonballs cannot compare. This is what the most skilled calendar-makers cannot calculate and the most eloquent cannot explain. The unreasonableness of heaven’s revolution does not deserve much argument. Now let me ask you: when the people of the world talk of heaven and earth, do they not take the earth’s realm to be the exact centre of the empty realm, enclosed by the three luminaries?”

paragraphs.orig: ## 4. 하늘과 별의 세계
paragraphs.en: 4. The Heavens and the Worlds of the Stars

paragraphs.orig: 虛子曰。七政包地。測候有據。地之正中。宜若無疑然。實翁曰。不然。滿天星宿。無非界也。自星界觀之。地界亦星也。無量之界。散處空界。惟此地界。巧居正中。無有是理。是以無非界也。無非轉也。衆界之觀。同於地觀。各自謂中。各星衆界。若七政包地。地測固然。以地謂七政之中則可。謂之衆星之正中則坐井之見也。是以七政之體。自轉如車輪。周包如磨驢。自地界觀之。近地而人見大者。謂之日月。遠地而人見小者。謂之五星。其實俱星界也。盖五緯包日而以日爲心。日月包地而以地爲心。金水近於日。故地月在包圈之外。三緯遠於日。故地月在包圈之內。金水之內。數十小星。並心於日。三緯之旁。四五小星。並心於各緯。地觀如是。各界之觀。可類而推。是以地爲兩曜之中而不得爲五緯之中。日爲五緯之中而不得爲衆星之正中。日且不得爲正中。况於地乎。

paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “The seven governors enclose the earth; observation bears this out. That the earth is at the exact centre seems beyond doubt.” Sirong said, “Not so. All the stars filling the heavens are worlds. Seen from a star-world, the earth-world is also a star. Innumerable worlds are scattered through the empty realm; for just this earth-world to occupy the exact centre by chance is unreasonable. Hence there is nothing that is not a world and nothing that does not turn. The view from the many worlds is the same as the view from the earth; each calls itself the centre. For each star and world it is as with the seven governors enclosing the earth: what the earth observes is naturally so. To call the earth the centre of the seven governors is allowable; to call it the exact centre of the many stars is the view of one sitting in a well. Hence the bodies of the seven governors rotate on themselves like cartwheels and enclose around like millstones. Seen from the earth, those near the earth that people see as large are called the sun and moon; those far from the earth that people see as small are called the five stars. In fact they are all star-worlds. The five planets enclose the sun and take the sun as their centre; the sun and moon enclose the earth and take the earth as their centre. Venus and Mercury are near the sun, so the earth and moon lie outside the circles they enclose; the three outer planets are far from the sun, so the earth and moon lie inside the circles they enclose. Within Venus and Mercury, dozens of small stars share the sun as their centre; beside the three outer planets, four or five small stars each share a planet as their centre. The earth’s view is thus; the views of the other worlds can be inferred by analogy. Therefore the earth can be the centre of the two luminaries but cannot be the centre of the five planets; the sun can be the centre of the five planets but cannot be the exact centre of the many stars. If even the sun cannot be the exact centre, how much less the earth?”

paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “I respectfully accept that the earth is not the centre. May I ask what world the Milky Way is?” Sirong said, “The Milky Way gathers many worlds to make a world, wheeling in a circle through the empty realm to form one great ring. Within the ring are many worlds, tens of millions in number; the sun, the earth and the other worlds are only one among them. This is one great world of the Great Void. Even so, this is how the earth sees it; beyond what the earth sees, there are worlds like the Milky Way of which we know not how many tens of millions or hundreds of millions. One must not rely on my tiny eyes and conclude hastily that the Milky Way is the foremost great world. Thus there are bright worlds, dark worlds, warm worlds and cold worlds. Those near bright worlds receive brightness and are bright; those near warm worlds receive warmth and are warm. The bright and warm is the sun-world; the dark and cold are the earth and moon. That the dark and cold become bright and warm is because the earth and moon are near the sun and receive it from it.”

paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “The many stars are all worlds. Can I hear in full of the shapes, colours and conditions of each world?” Sirong laughed and said, “Shao Yaofu said that heaven and earth have opening and closing, and set the limit of opening and closing at one epoch of one hundred and twenty-nine thousand six hundred years. He thought it a grand view, and the world too has expected it to be a grand view. What do you make of it?” Heoja said, “As for the limit of opening and closing, I have heard the theory but cannot believe its principle.”

paragraphs.orig: 實翁曰然。物之有體質者。終必有壞。凝以成質。融以反氣。地之有閉闢。其理固也。惟天者虛氣。蕩蕩灝灝。無形無眹。開成何物。閉成何物。不思甚矣。夫吾之出世。計以一元。不知其爲幾千萬億。周遊各界。閱其凝融。又不知其爲幾千萬億。前乎吾者。又不知其爲幾千萬億。後乎吾者。又不知其爲幾千萬億。是以各界之形色情狀。爾所不能知。亦所不必知。吾所不能言。亦所不必言。設或言之。爾必驚疑。無所徵信。今此據爾之所視。語爾之所知。

paragraphs.en: Sirong said, “Yes. Whatever has bodily substance must in the end decay: condensing, it becomes substance; melting, it returns to qi. That the earth has closing and opening is certainly in its principle. But heaven is void qi, broad and boundless, without form or sign; what would it open into, what would it close into? How thoughtless! As for my coming into the world, reckoned in epochs it is I know not how many tens of millions or hundreds of millions; roaming round the worlds and watching their condensing and melting, I know not how many tens of millions or hundreds of millions more; those before me are I know not how many tens of millions or hundreds of millions, and those after me are I know not how many tens of millions or hundreds of millions. Hence the shapes, colours and conditions of the various worlds are what you cannot know and need not know, and what I cannot tell and need not tell. Even if I told you, you would be startled and doubtful, with nothing to confirm it. So now, on the basis of what you see, I shall tell you what you already know.”

paragraphs.orig: 日者體大於地。其數多倍。其質火。其色赤。質火故其性溫。色赤故其光明。焰煇四發。漸遠而漸微。極於數千萬里。生於本界者。禀受純火。其體晃朗。其性剛烈。其知烱透。其氣飛揚。無晝夜之分。無冬夏之候。終古居火而不覺其溫也。
paragraphs.reading: 일자체대어지. 기수다배. 기질화. 기색적. 질화고기성온. 색적고기광명. 염휘사발. 점원이점미. 극어수천만리. 생어본계자. 품수순화. 기체황랑. 기성강렬. 기지경투. 기기비양. 무주야지분. 무동하지후. 종고거화이불각기온야.
paragraphs.en: The sun’s body is larger than the earth, by many times. Its substance is fire, and its colour is red. Because its substance is fire, its nature is warm; because its colour is red, its light is bright. Flames and radiance burst out on all sides, growing fainter as they go farther, and reaching as far as tens of millions of li. Those born in its own world receive pure fire: their bodies are dazzling and clear, their natures fierce, their awareness bright and penetrating, their qi soaring. There is no division of day and night and no seasons of winter and summer; through all ages they dwell in fire and do not feel its warmth.

paragraphs.orig: 月者體小於地。三十居一。其質氷。其色淸。質氷故其性冷。色淸故暎日發光。遠日則凝。空明如鏡。近日則融。汪洋如海。生於本界者。禀受純氷。其體瀅澈。其性潔凈。其知澄明。其氣輕浮。晝夜之分。冬夏之候。與地界同。終古居氷而不覺其冷也。

paragraphs.en: The moon’s body is smaller than the earth, one thirtieth of it. Its substance is ice, and its colour is clear. Because its substance is ice, its nature is cold; because its colour is clear, it reflects the sun and gives off light. Far from the sun it congeals, empty and bright as a mirror; near the sun it melts, vast like a sea. Those born in its own world receive pure ice: their bodies are crystal clear, their natures pure, their awareness limpid, their qi light and buoyant. Day and night, winter and summer are the same as in the earth-world. Through all ages they dwell in ice and do not feel its cold.

paragraphs.orig: 地者七政之滓穢。其質氷土。其色晦濁。質氷土故其性寒。色晦濁故映日少。光近而受溫。土潤氷解。生於本界者。其軆厖駁。其性粗雜。其知昏憨。其氣鈍滯。日照而爲晝。日隱而爲夜。日近而爲夏。日遠而爲冬。日火蒸炙。滋產衆生。形交胎產。人物繁衆。神智日閉。小慧日長。利慾淫熬。生滅芒忽。此地界之情狀而爾之所知也。

paragraphs.en: The earth is the dregs and filth of the seven governors. Its substance is ice and soil, and its colour is dim and turbid. Because its substance is ice and soil, its nature is cold; because its colour is dim and turbid, it reflects little of the sun. Near the light it receives warmth; the soil moistens and the ice melts. Those born in its own world are of mottled and coarse body, crude and mixed in nature, dull and foolish in awareness, sluggish and stagnant in qi. When the sun shines it is day; when the sun hides it is night; when the sun is near it is summer; when the sun is far it is winter. The heat of the sun steams and bakes, breeding the multitude of beings; through coupling and gestation humans and things multiply. Spirit and wisdom are closed off day by day while petty cleverness grows day by day; fired by desire for gain and lust, they are born and die in a flash. Such is the condition of the earth-world, which you already know.

paragraphs.orig: 虛子曰。居日界者。如火鼠之居火。居月界者。如水族之居水。其理然也。敢問兩界之生。可通其遊歷歟。

paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “Those who dwell in the sun-world are like fire-rats dwelling in fire; those who dwell in the moon-world are like aquatic creatures dwelling in water. This accords with reason. May I ask, can the living beings of the two worlds travel to one another?”

paragraphs.orig: 實翁曰。何言之愚也。陸居者入水則窒死。水居者出陸則喘死。南人不耐寒。北人不耐暑。一界之中。尙不能通。各界之生。形氣絶異。有如水火。水火之同器。豈有其理乎。

paragraphs.en: Sirong said, “How foolish of you to say so! Land-dwellers suffocate if they enter water; water-dwellers gasp to death if they leave the land. Southerners cannot endure cold, northerners cannot endure heat. Within a single world they still cannot interchange; the beings of the various worlds differ utterly in form and qi, as fire and water do. Is there any reason for fire and water to share one vessel?”

paragraphs.orig: 虛子曰。虛子濁界之物也。聞夫子之言。始知太虛之間有此衆界。願賴神力。陞彼九霄。遊歷太虛。今日月之界。尙不相通。將小子終不免芒忽於濁界也。

paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “I, Heoja, am a creature of the turbid world. Hearing your words, Master, I first realised that in the Great Void there are these many worlds. I wish to rely on spirit power to ascend those nine heavens and roam the Great Void. But if even the worlds of the sun and moon cannot reach each other, then I, your little disciple, will never escape vanishing in a flash in the turbid world.”

paragraphs.orig: 實翁笑曰。爾果欲陞彼九霄。不患無術。盖池魚成龍。溟鯤化鵬。壤蟲蟬蛻。野蠶蝶幻。人之靈巧。何患無術。十年胎息。丹成脫殼。法身靈變。超越雲霄。不焦於火。不濡於水。遊歷衆界。永享淸快。爾欲爲之乎。

paragraphs.en: Sirong laughed and said, “If you truly wish to ascend those nine heavens, you need not worry about lacking a method. A pond fish becomes a dragon; the great Kun of the dark sea transforms into the Peng; earth grubs moult into cicadas; field silkworms change into butterflies. With human spiritual skill, why worry about lacking a method? Ten years of embryonic breathing; when the elixir is made, you shed your shell; the dharma-body changes spiritually and surpasses clouds and sky, unscorched by fire, undampened by water, roaming the many worlds and enjoying eternal clarity and joy. Do you wish to do it?”

paragraphs.orig: 虛子曰。此世俗所謂仙人之術也。小子聞其說而不敢信也。果有此術。棄妻子如弊屣也。

paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “That is what the vulgar call the art of the immortals. I have heard of it, but do not dare believe it. If there truly were such an art, I would cast away wife and children like worn-out sandals.”

paragraphs.orig: 實翁厲聲曰。吾以汝爲可敎也。乃愚滯之難啓。利慾之難淸。有如是乎。彼胎丹之術。實有其理。亦有其人。雖然。久則萬年。少則千年。終歸消滅。亦何益哉。
paragraphs.reading: 실옹여성왈. 오이여위가교야. 내우체지난계. 이욕지난청. 유여시호. 피태단지술. 실유기리. 역유기인. 수연. 구칙만년. 소칙천년. 종귀소멸. 역하익재.
paragraphs.en: Sirong said sternly, “I thought you could be taught. Is it so hard to open a dull and stagnant mind, so hard to purge desire for gain? That art of the embryo and elixir truly has its principle, and there are indeed such people. Even so, at longest ten thousand years, at least a thousand, they all end in extinction. What benefit is there in that?

paragraphs.orig: 人之生世也。願慾無極。華美之奉。靡曼之色。崇高之位。燀赫之權。珍恠之物。詭異之觀。人皆慕之。其巧且黠者。念其憂危。苦其訿議。患其芒忽。又知其不可必得。則乃反身淸修。逞慾於象外。以圖萬千年淸快。及其仙昇。神思窈冥。遊歷衆界。七情永閟。耳如無聞。目如無見。參以俗情。無一樂事。衆生見其飛昇度世。以世情妄意。仙人乘龍御風。招呼仙侶。遊戱異境。備諸快樂。不亦愚乎。

paragraphs.en: “When people live in the world, their wishes and desires are limitless: sumptuous offerings, voluptuous beauty, lofty rank, blazing power, rare and strange objects, bizarre sights. Everyone longs for them. Those among them who are clever and sly, thinking of their anxieties and perils, pained by slander, troubled by the fleetingness of life, and knowing too that these things cannot be surely obtained, turn back upon themselves to cultivate purity, indulging their desires beyond the realm of forms in order to seek ten thousand years of clarity and joy. When they ascend as immortals, their spirit and thought are dim and remote; they roam the many worlds, the seven emotions sealed for ever, their ears as if hearing nothing, their eyes as if seeing nothing. Set against worldly feeling, there is not a single pleasant thing in it. Yet the multitude, seeing them fly up and pass beyond the world, project worldly feelings and imagine that the immortals ride dragons and drive the wind, call to immortal companions, play in strange realms, and enjoy all pleasures. Is this not foolish?

paragraphs.orig: 夫仙人之術。要在無爲。恬恬漠漠。凈靜不撓。艶樂俗情。一萌于中。眞元渙散。法身墮落。苟令世人之慕仙者。置之此境。必將厭其寥廓。苦其簡泊。不欲斯須居也。且世人或有爲幻妄之術者。托以眞仙。閃忽詭奇。以弄愚俗。愚俗之妄慕。實由於此。夫眞仙。飄颻遺世。忘親戚之恩。絶舊鄕之戀。况濁界臭穢。不可嚮邇。豈其辱身降志。挾術驚世。透露光景。自作罪過。甚矣。地界之愚昏也。是以仙昇之徒。無營無欲。以葆眞精。萬千年間。終歸消滅。畢竟就盡。久速無分。石火泡幻。實同殤子。原其發願。實由利心而卒無其利。巧而實拙。黠而實愚。爾欲學道而乃有是願。不亦悞乎。

paragraphs.en: “The art of the immortals consists in non-action: placid and tranquil, pure and still, unperturbed. Once the feelings of seductive pleasure and worldly sentiment sprout within, the true origin disperses and the dharma-body falls. If the people of the world who admire immortals were put in this state, they would surely find it desolate and vast, be pained by its simplicity and bareness, and not wish to stay even a moment. Moreover, there are people in the world who practise illusory arts and pretend to be true immortals, flashing and uncanny, to make fools of the ignorant mob; the ignorant mob’s wild admiration really stems from this. A true immortal drifts free of the world, forgetting the kindness of kin and severing longing for his old home; how much less would he draw near the foul turbid world! Would he disgrace himself and lower his purpose, flaunt his art to startle the world, reveal his glimmers, and bring offence upon himself? How deep the folly and dimness of the earth-world! Therefore those who ascend as immortals have no scheming and no desires, preserving the true essence; but after tens of thousands of years they too end in extinction, finished utterly. Long or brief makes no difference: a spark from flint, a bubble, an illusion; they are truly the same as a child who died young. Tracing their vow back, it arises from a heart for gain and in the end yields no gain: clever yet in truth clumsy, sly yet in truth foolish. You wish to study the Way and yet hold such a wish. Is that not a mistake?”

paragraphs.orig: 虛子霍然而悟。犁然而笑曰。小子過矣。敢問各界俱轉。亦能周包他界。獨此地界。只能自轉。不能周行。何也。實翁曰。衆界之成。體有輕重。性有鈍疾。輕而疾者。轉而能周。重而鈍者。轉而不周。輕疾之極。周圈極濶。三緯之類也。重鈍之極。周圈切面。地界之類也。輕界之生。虛而靈。重界之生。實而滯。

paragraphs.en: Heoja suddenly awakened and laughed in clear understanding: “I was in the wrong. May I ask: all worlds rotate and can also enclose other worlds; why does only this earth-world merely rotate on itself, and not travel around?” Sirong said, “In the formation of worlds, bodies differ in lightness and weight and natures in dullness and speed. Those light and swift rotate and can circle round; those heavy and dull rotate and cannot circle. At the extreme of lightness and swiftness, the orbit is vast; such are the three outer planets. At the extreme of heaviness and dullness, the orbit hugs the surface; the earth-world is of this kind. The beings of light worlds are void and spiritual; the beings of heavy worlds are solid and sluggish.”

paragraphs.orig: 虛子曰。然則五緯。五行之精也。恒星。衆物之象也。下應地界。妖祥有徵。何也。

paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “Then the five planets are the essences of the Five Phases, and the fixed stars are the images of the many things, responding to the earth-world below with omens that have signs. How so?”

paragraphs.orig: 實翁曰。五星之體。各有其德。五行之分屬。術家之陋也。且自地界觀之。繁星連絡。如昴宿之叢萃。類居羣聚。其實十數點之中。高下遠近。不啻千萬其里。自彼界觀之。日月地三點。耿耿如連珠。今以日月地。舍爲一物而命之以三星。可乎。惟曆象推步。資於宮度。星之有名。曆家之權定也。乃若繁衍牽合。參以俗事。轉作術家之欛柄。支離乖妄。極於分野。夫地界之於太虛。不啻微塵爾。中國之於地界。十數分之一爾。以周地之界。分屬宿度。猶或有說。以九州之偏。硬配衆界。分合傅會。窺覘灾瑞。妄而又妄。不足道也。

paragraphs.en: Sirong said, “Each of the five stars’ bodies has its own virtue. Assigning them to the Five Phases is the crudity of the diviners. Moreover, seen from the earth-world, the dense stars link together, like the Pleiades clustering, kinds dwelling in groups; in fact, among a dozen or so points, high and low, near and far differ by more than ten million li. Seen from another world, the three points of sun, moon and earth shine like a string of pearls; now if one lumped sun, moon and earth into a single thing and called it ‘the three stars,’ would that do? Calendar and calculation depend on the degrees of the lodgings; the naming of stars is a provisional convention of the calendar-makers. But when it was elaborated, forced into correlations, and mixed with worldly affairs, it was turned into a handle for the diviners, and its fragmented absurdities reached their extreme in the field-allocation system. The earth-world is, to the Great Void, no more than a speck of dust; China is, to the earth-world, about a tenth part or so. To assign the world around the earth to the lodgings and degrees might still be defensible; but to force the corner of the Nine Provinces to match the many worlds, joining and separating by false analogy to spy out calamity and omen, is absurd upon absurd and not worth speaking of.”

paragraphs.orig: 虛子曰。然則分野之說。流傳已久。或有明徵。好風好雨。塋惑守心。凡乾象之符應。皆不足信乎。

paragraphs.orig: 實翁曰。衆口鑠金。積毁銷骨。口不可鑠金。毁不可銷骨。猶致銷鑠者。人衆而勝天也。技術雖妄。人心有感。依信之極。或致徵應。此撮空之虛影也。眩於虛影。不察情實。惑之甚矣。且箕風畢雨。因其俗諺。借明民情。非謂兩星眞有是好。若熒惑之行。時有包旋。留守進退。緣於地觀。天高聽卑。司星之謬也。

paragraphs.en: Sirong said, “‘The mouths of the many can melt metal; accumulated slander can dissolve bones.’ A mouth cannot melt metal and slander cannot dissolve bones, yet they bring about melting and dissolving because people are many and overcome heaven. Arts may be false, but the human heart has resonance; at the extreme of reliance and belief, a response may sometimes occur. This is a vain shadow grasped out of empty air. To be dazzled by a vain shadow and not examine the true facts is the extreme of delusion. As for the wind of the Winnowing Basket and the rain of the Net, they follow popular sayings, borrowed to make clear the feelings of the people; it does not mean that the two stars truly have such likings. As for the movement of Mars, it sometimes makes encircling turns, lingering and keeping, advancing and retreating, owing to the earth’s viewpoint. ‘Heaven is high yet hears what is low’ is the error of the star-keepers.”

paragraphs.orig: 虛子曰。月中明暗。或謂水土。或爲地影。願聞其說。實翁曰。吾語其實。爾信吾口。不若據爾所見。開爾實見。夫鄙諺所謂桂兎。東昇之望形也。苟其水土也。月之中天。其形必橫。月之西落。其形必倒。今乃隨行而隨變。不橫不倒。化成各形。三停之形。終古如一。且觀弦月。宜見其半而全形備焉。特其蹙而狹爾。水土之說。似是而實非。盖月體如鏡。地界半面。隨明透影。東昇之影。東界之半面也。中天之影。中界之半面也。西落之影。西界之半面也。謂之地影。不亦可乎。

paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “As for the light and dark in the moon, some say it is water and earth, some say it is the earth’s shadow. I wish to hear your account.” Sirong said, “I tell you the facts; but rather than trust my mouth, you had better rely on what you see and open your own true sight. The common saying about the cassia tree and the rabbit refers to the form seen at the rising of the full moon in the east. If it were water and earth, then when the moon is at mid-sky its form would have to be sideways, and when the moon sets in the west its form would have to be upside down. But now it changes along with its course, neither sideways nor upside down, taking various forms, while the form at each of the three stations stays always the same. And look at the half moon: one ought to see its half, yet the whole form is complete, only contracted and narrow. The water-and-earth theory seems right but is actually wrong. The moon’s body is like a mirror: the half-face of the earth-world shows through as a shadow in accordance with the light. The shadow when rising in the east is the half-face of the eastern world; the shadow at mid-sky is the half-face of the central world; the shadow at setting in the west is the half-face of the western world. Might it not rightly be called the earth’s shadow?”

paragraphs.orig: 虛子曰。敢問天之有兩極。何也。實翁曰。地界之人。不知地轉。故謂天有兩極。其實非天之極也。乃地之極也。凡物之轉動。由於虛實而身外有界耳。今夫天者其體至虛。其性至靜。其大無量。其塞無間。雖欲轉動。得乎。惟星宿衆界。各有轉動。歲次之論。所由起也。其轉動之勢。各有遲速。南北東西。遊移無定。特以距地絶遠。視差甚微。圖象隨時。稽古無憑。人自不覺爾。

paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “May I ask why heaven has two poles?” Sirong said, “Because the people of the earth-world do not know that the earth turns, they say that heaven has two poles. In fact they are not the poles of heaven but the poles of the earth. For all things that rotate, rotation arises from there being solid and void, with a boundary beyond the body. Now heaven is utterly void in body and utterly still in nature, its size immeasurable, filling without a gap; though it wished to rotate, could it? Only the stars and the many worlds each rotate, and hence arose the discussion of the year-stations. Their rotating motions differ in slowness and swiftness, wandering irregularly south, north, east and west; but because they are extremely far from the earth, the parallax is very slight, the charts vary with the times, the ancient records offer no evidence, and people simply do not notice.”

paragraphs.orig: 虛子曰。敢問流妖彗孛。何氣致然。實翁曰。此不一端。有凝合於空界而成者。有各界之氣相盪而成者。有融界之餘氣流走而成者。此皆所以然而致也。惟人地之氣。極其和而成者。慶星之類也。人地之氣。失其常而成者。彗孛之類也。

paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “May I ask what qi causes shooting stars, ominous stars, comets and bushy stars?” Sirong said, “These are not of a single kind. Some form by condensing and combining in the empty realm; some form by the qi of various worlds colliding; some form by the leftover qi of melting worlds flowing off. All come about for these reasons. Those formed when the qi of humans and earth reaches its utmost harmony are of the type of the auspicious stars; those formed when the qi of humans and earth loses its constancy are of the type of comets and bushy stars.”

paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “Venus is seen at noon; is it the fullness of its radiant qi? May I ask, does the qi of the worlds wax and wane at times?” Sirong said, “Venus encircles the sun, its orbit lying half outside the sun and half inside. The part outside is farther from the earth; the part inside is nearer to the earth. Moreover, Venus has no light of its own but receives brightness from the sun, and has phases like the moon. When it is near the earth and its brightness is full on the side facing down, its light is strong on the earth and the sun cannot overpower it. It is not that its body waxes and wanes.”

paragraphs.en: Sirong said, “Being bound to yin and yang and mired in moral principle, failing to observe the Way of Heaven: this is the fault of the earlier Confucians. When the moon covers the sun, the sun is eclipsed by it; when the earth covers the moon, the moon is eclipsed by it. When their longitude and latitude coincide and the three worlds line up, they cover one another and eclipse occurs; this is their regular motion. Moreover, the sun is eclipsed in the earth-world while the earth is eclipsed in the moon-world; the moon is eclipsed in the earth-world while the sun is eclipsed in the moon-world. This is the constant course of the three worlds and has no connection with order or disorder in the earth-world. Even so, when the sun sets and it becomes night, that too is a change of the sun; if one conducts oneself at night as one does by day, there will be disorder. An eclipse as a change is likewise. To meet a change by cultivating oneself and examining oneself is only proper in human affairs.”

paragraphs.orig: ## 5. 날씨와 계절
paragraphs.en: 5. Weather and the Seasons

paragraphs.orig: 虛子曰。風雲雨雪霜雹雷霆虹暈凡天道之變。可得悉聞歟。實翁曰。虛者天也。是以井坎之空。甁罌之空。亦天也。凡風雲之屬。皆出於虛。故謂之道。其實地氣之蒸成。不專於天也。嘗試言之。風者生於地角。地之轉也。不能無掀搖。山嶺之高。隧壑之深。不能無激盪。故虛氣簸漾。四出而爲風。激之急者其風猛。激之徐者其風緩。近於激者其勢大。遠於激者其勢微。一激之後。互相衝撞。東西南北。任其驅射。且蛟龍之騰化。雷雨之翻注。亦能煽呼。皆出於地面。是以離地數百里。未嘗有風焉。雲者。山川之氣騰結而成形。其色本淡。借日光以成雜采。日午多白。正受光也。其黑者。積厚而陰也。朝夕多紅紫。地氣之盪日也。

paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “Wind, cloud, rain, snow, frost, hail, thunder, lightning, rainbow, halo: all the changes of the Way of Heaven; can I hear them all?” Sirong said, “The void is heaven. Hence the emptiness of wells and pits, of jars and bottles, is also heaven. Wind, clouds and the like all come out of the void, and so they are called the Way. In fact they are formed by the steaming of the earth’s qi and do not belong exclusively to heaven. Let me try to explain. Wind arises from the corners of the earth. The earth cannot turn without shaking and swaying, and the height of mountain ridges and the depth of ravines cannot but stir up turbulence. Hence the void qi billows and surges out in all directions as wind. Where the stirring is sharp the wind is fierce; where it is slow the wind is gentle. Near the stirring its force is great; far from it its force is slight. After one stirring, the winds collide with one another and race off in any direction, east, west, south or north. Moreover, the soaring and transforming of dragons and the pouring down of thunderstorms can also fan up wind; all arise from the earth’s surface. Hence, several hundred li above the earth there has never been any wind. Clouds are the qi of mountains and rivers rising and congealing into form. Their colour is originally pale; they borrow sunlight to make mixed hues. At noon they are mostly white, receiving the light directly; the black ones are thick with accumulation and in shade. At dawn and dusk they are mostly red and purple, owing to the earth’s qi stirring the sun.

paragraphs.orig: 雨者。甑露之勢也。水土之氣蒸騰于空。鬱于密雲。無所泄而凝成。氣蒸而雲不密則不成雨。雲密而氣不蒸則亦不成雨。雪者。冷氣之蒸也。霜者。溫冷之襍也。雹者。溫冷相薄。急雨之凍也。皆成於蒸氣。雨之類也。

paragraphs.en: “Rain is the working of dew in a steamer. The qi of water and soil steams up into the void and is bottled up in dense clouds; having nowhere to escape, it condenses. If the qi steams but the clouds are not dense, no rain forms; if the clouds are dense but the qi does not steam, again no rain forms. Snow is the steaming of cold qi. Frost is a mixture of warmth and cold. Hail is warmth and cold pressing against each other, a sudden rain frozen. All are formed from steam qi and are of the same kind as rain.

paragraphs.orig: 雷者。蒸氣隔鬱。相撞發火。電者其光也。雷者其聲也。火之所觸。物必靡爛。先電而後雷者。發於遠也。電雷並作者。發於近也。遠於地者。散於空界。近於地者。觸而震物。不雷而電者。百里以遠也。不電而雷者。積雲之隔也。鐵鎌扣石。火鈴布地。違避堅濕。必就燥絨。蓋堅濕者。火之所畏。燥絨者。火之所嗜。夫雷者。其性剛烈。其氣奮猛。違避正直。必就邪沴。蓋正直者。雷之所畏。邪沴者。雷之所嗜。夫人之靈覺。乃一身之火精。况雷者。天地之正火。剛烈奮猛。好生嫉惡。翣時暴霆。靈覺如神。凡人物被震。時顯奇跡。曲施機巧。是雷神之有情也。火精靈覺。實同人心。虹者。水氣也。朝東夕西。借日以成。日之斜射。必成半規。日午無虹。水氣不厚也。日月之暈。虹之類也。成於空故必成全規。虹暈之成規。日月之圓也。

paragraphs.en: “Thunder is when steam qi, shut in and bottled up, collides and strikes fire. Lightning is its light; thunder is its sound. Where the fire strikes, things surely crumble and rot. When lightning comes first and thunder after, it was emitted far away; when lightning and thunder occur together, it was emitted near. What is far from the earth scatters in the empty realm; what is near the earth strikes and shakes things. Lightning without thunder is more than a hundred li away; thunder without lightning is due to a screen of piled clouds. When an iron sickle strikes stone, the sparks scatter over the ground; they avoid what is hard and damp and invariably go to dry tinder. For the hard and damp is what fire fears; dry fluff is what fire relishes. Thunder, for its part, is fierce in nature and furious in qi; it avoids the upright and invariably goes to the crooked and malign. For the upright is what thunder fears; the crooked and malign is what thunder relishes. The spiritual awareness of humans is the fire-essence of the whole body; how much more is thunder the true fire of heaven and earth, fierce and violent, loving life and hating evil! Its sudden crash comes in an instant, its spiritual awareness godlike. When humans and things are struck by it, they often show strange traces, as if some cunning had been applied to them point by point; this shows that the thunder spirit has feelings. The awareness of the fire-essence is truly the same as the human heart. A rainbow is water vapour. It is in the east in the morning and in the west in the evening, formed by borrowing the sun. When the sun shines obliquely, it surely forms a half-circle; there is no rainbow at noon because the water vapour is not thick. The halos of the sun and moon are of the rainbow kind; formed in the void, they must form a full circle. That rainbows and halos form circles is because the sun and moon are round.”

paragraphs.orig: 虛子曰。人在地上。見天未半。雖然。或日已東昇而西見月食。且日月之在地面。距人遠而圈徑必大。其在中天。距人近而圈徑反小。何也。

paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “Standing on the earth, one sees less than half the sky. Even so, sometimes when the sun has already risen in the east, a lunar eclipse is seen in the west. Moreover, when the sun and moon are at the horizon, they are far from the observer, yet the diameter of their disks must be large; at mid-sky they are near the observer, yet the diameter is on the contrary small. Why?”

paragraphs.orig: 實翁曰。此氣之所爲也。試將銅錢置于浴盤。退而窺之。纔見一點。及灌注淸水。全形騰露。此水之力也。玻瓈籠眼。秋毫如指。此玻瓈之力也。今水土之氣。蒸包地面。外嫋三光。內眩人目。映發如水。靉靆如玻瓈。騰卑爲高。幼小爲大。西洋之人。有見於此。命以淸蒙。仰測見小。淸蒙之薄也。橫望見大。淸蒙之厚也。夫雷聲之壯而不過百里。銃丸之猛而不及千步。此遠近之勢也。雖然。遠近之所以致然。必有其故。盖遊氣充塞。穿撥有限。聲馳丸走。力竭而止。人之目力。亦猶是也。夫日月眞徑。終不可測也。月體初朏。明飽魄外。是光燄成暈。非月本體。弦望徑圍。靡所適從。况太陽純火。燄暈倍大。眞界深淺。竟無槩量。且測望圜體。近則見小。遠則見大。彈丸之微。莫辨本形。况於日月乎。

paragraphs.en: Sirong said, “This is the doing of qi. Try putting a copper coin in a washbasin and stepping back to peer at it: you see only a point. But when clear water is poured in, the whole shape rises into view. That is the power of the water. When glass is set over the eye, a fine hair looks like a finger. That is the power of the glass. Now the qi of water and earth steams and envelops the earth’s surface; outside it wreathes the three luminaries, inside it dazzles human eyes, shining like water and hazy like glass, raising the low into the high and the small into the large. Westerners, seeing this, named it the ‘clear haze.’ Looking up, things appear small because the clear haze is thin; looking horizontally, things appear large because the clear haze is thick. The roar of thunder carries no more than a hundred li; the fierce cannonball does not reach a thousand paces. This is the effect of distance. Even so, there must be a reason why distance causes this: the drifting qi fills all space, and the extent to which anything can pierce through and push it aside is limited; sound races and shot flies until their strength is exhausted and then stop. The power of the human eye is likewise. The true diameters of the sun and moon can never be measured. When the moon is a new crescent, its brightness is full beyond the dark part; this is the flare of light forming a halo and is not the moon’s own body. As for its diameter at the quarter and the full, there is nothing to go by. How much more so for the sun, pure fire, whose flame-halo is twice as large; the true depth of its realm cannot be gauged at all. Moreover, in observing a round body, near it looks small and far it looks large; with something as tiny as a pellet one cannot tell its true shape. How much less the sun and moon?”

paragraphs.orig: 虛子曰。地體之圓。分野之妄。旣得聞命矣。敢問一日之間朝晝異候。一歲之中冬夏異候。一地之中南北異候。何也。

paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “That the earth’s body is round and that field-allocation is false, I have now heard. May I ask why the weather differs between morning and noon in a single day, between winter and summer in a single year, and between south and north in a single land?”

paragraphs.orig: 實翁曰。冷者。地界之本氣也。溫者。日火之熏炙也。且以中國言之。北京北至之日。不及天頂十六度。日光微斜。溫候已减。從此以北至于極下。則夏候如冬候。若其冬候。土地凍坼。有氷無水。南海北至之日。正當天頂。夏日直射。烈炎如焚。終古無氷。從此以南至赤道南二十餘度。一歲溫候。互有消長。惟赤道南北。冬夏易其候。赤道南數十度。以南至爲夏。以北至爲冬。其溫冷之候。畧同中國。由此益南至極下。則夏候如冬。若其冬候。土地凍坼。有氷無水。亦如北極之下。由南極而南。由北極而北。其漸溫漸冷。極溫極冷幷同。此地界惟南北易其候而已。

paragraphs.en: Sirong said, “Cold is the native qi of the earth-world; warmth is the scorching of the sun’s fire. Take China as an example. On the day the sun reaches its northern limit, at Beijing the sun falls sixteen degrees short of the zenith; the sunlight is slightly slanted, and the warmth is already reduced. From here north to the pole, the summer weather is like winter; and as for the winter weather, the ground freezes and cracks, and there is ice but no water. At the Southern Sea, on the day the sun reaches its northern limit, the sun is exactly at the zenith; the summer sun shines straight down, blazing like a conflagration, and there is no ice ever. From here south to more than twenty degrees south of the equator, the warmth in the course of a year waxes and wanes in turn. Only north and south of the equator are summer and winter exchanged in their weather. A few dozen degrees south of the equator, the southern solstice is summer and the northern solstice is winter; their conditions of warmth and cold are roughly like those of China. Going farther south from here to the pole, the summer weather is like winter; and as for the winter weather, the ground freezes and cracks, and there is ice but no water, as under the North Pole. Going south from the South Pole and north from the North Pole, the gradual warming and cooling and the extremes of heat and cold are all alike. Thus in the earth-world it is only north and south that exchange their weather.

paragraphs.orig: 盖日由黃道。出入於赤道。內外各二十三度。地界之近赤道而日光直射者。其氣極溫。稍遠於赤道而日光斜射者。其氣微溫。絶遠於赤道而日光橫射者。其氣極冷。是以地之有溫。受於日也。溫有微極。日之斜直也。察乎此則朝晝之異候明矣。朝晝之異候明。則冬夏之異候明矣。冬夏之異候旣明。則南北之異候亦明矣。

paragraphs.en: “The sun travels along the ecliptic, going in and out of the equator, twenty-three degrees to either side. Places on the earth near the equator where the sunlight falls straight are extremely warm; places somewhat farther from the equator where the sunlight falls obliquely are mildly warm; places very far from the equator where the sunlight falls grazing are extremely cold. Hence the earth’s having warmth is from receiving it from the sun; that the warmth is slight or extreme depends on whether the sun is oblique or straight. Examine this, and the differing weather of morning and noon becomes clear; when the differing weather of morning and noon is clear, the differing weather of winter and summer is clear; once the differing weather of winter and summer is clear, the differing weather of south and north is also clear.”

paragraphs.orig: 虛子曰。日南至而一陽生。日北至而一陰生。陰陽交而爲春夏。天地閉而爲秋冬。南陽而北陰。地勢之定局也。夏溫而冬冷。陰陽之交閉也。今夫子舍陰陽之定局。去交閉之眞機。率之以日火之遠近斜直。無乃不可乎。

paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “When the sun reaches the south, one yang is born; when the sun reaches the north, one yin is born. Yin and yang intermingle and it becomes spring and summer; heaven and earth are closed and it becomes autumn and winter. South yang and north yin is the fixed arrangement of the configuration of the earth. Summer warm and winter cold is the intermingling and closing of yin and yang. Now you, Master, abandon the fixed arrangement of yin and yang, discard the true workings of intermingling and closing, and reduce everything to the nearness, farness, obliqueness and straightness of the sun’s fire. Is that not unacceptable?”

paragraphs.orig: 實翁曰。然。有是言也。雖然。陽之類有萬而皆本於火。陰之類有萬而皆本於地。古之人有見於此而有陰陽之說。萬物化生於春夏則謂之交。萬物收藏於秋冬則謂之閉。古人立言。各有爲也。究其本則實屬於日火之淺深。非謂天地之間別有陰陽二氣隨時生伏主張造化。如後人之說也。

paragraphs.en: Sirong said, “Yes, there is such a saying. Even so, the kinds of yang are ten thousand yet all are rooted in fire; the kinds of yin are ten thousand yet all are rooted in earth. The ancients saw this and so had the theory of yin and yang. When the myriad things are born and transformed in spring and summer, it is called intermingling; when they are gathered and stored in autumn and winter, it is called closing. The ancients framed their words each for a purpose. Investigated to the root, it truly belongs to the shallowness or depth of the sun’s fire. It does not mean that between heaven and earth there are separate qi of yin and yang, arising and hiding according to the seasons and running the work of creation, as later people say.”

paragraphs.orig: ## 6. 오행설 비판과 바다·땅의 변화
paragraphs.en: 6. A Critique of the Five Phases, and the Changes of Sea and Land

paragraphs.orig: 虛子曰。地界生物。統屬於日火。假令日界一朝融滅。卽此地界將無一物。

paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “The living things of the earth-world all belong to the sun’s fire. Supposing the sun-world melted away in a single morning, this earth-world would at once have not a single thing.”

paragraphs.orig: 實翁曰。氷土相結。物不生成。暗冷混沌。成一死界。虛空之中。絶遠日火。徒成死界。奚啻千萬。

paragraphs.en: Sirong said, “With ice and soil bound together, things cannot be born and grow; dark and cold chaos makes a dead world. In the void, far from the sun’s fire, mere dead worlds are many, far more than ten million.”

paragraphs.orig: 虛子曰。天者五行之氣也。地者五行之質也。天有其氣。地有其質。物之生成。自有其具。豈其專屬於日乎。

paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “Heaven is the qi of the Five Phases; earth is their substance. Heaven has its qi and earth has its substance; the birth and growth of things naturally has its own means. How could it belong exclusively to the sun?”

paragraphs.orig: 實翁曰。虞夏言六府。水火金木土糓是也。易言八象。天地火水雷風山澤是也。洪範言五行。水火金木土是也。佛言四大。地水火風是也。古人隨時立言。以作萬物之總名。非謂不可加一。不可减一。天地萬物。適有此數也。故五行之數。原非定論。術家祖之。河洛以傅會之。易象以穿鑿之。生克飛伏。支離繚繞。張皇衆技。卒無其理。夫火者日也。水土者地也。若木金者。日地之所生成。不當與三者並立爲行也。且天者。淸虛之氣彌滿無際。其可以蕞爾地界之噓吸。擬議於至淸至虛之中乎。是知天者氣而已。日者火而已。地者水土而已。萬物者。氣之粕糟。火之陶鎔。地之疣贅。三者闕其一。不成造化。復何疑乎。

paragraphs.en: Sirong said, “The Books of Yu and Xia spoke of the six treasuries: water, fire, metal, wood, earth and grain. The Changes speaks of the eight images: heaven, earth, fire, water, thunder, wind, mountain and marsh. The Great Plan speaks of the five phases: water, fire, metal, wood and earth. Buddhism speaks of the four great elements: earth, water, fire and wind. The ancients spoke as the occasion required, to make a general name for the myriad things; they did not mean that one could not be added or one subtracted, or that heaven, earth and the myriad things happen to have just this number. So the number of the Five Phases was never a settled doctrine; the diviners took it as their ancestor, forcing it to fit the River Chart and the Luo Writing and drilling it into the images of the Changes. Their generation and overcoming, flying and hiding are fragmented and tangled, swaggering with a host of techniques, and in the end have no principle. Fire is the sun; water and earth are the earth. As for wood and metal, they are produced by the sun and the earth, and should not stand alongside the other three as phases. Moreover, heaven is a clear, void qi filling without limit; can the exhaling and inhaling of the petty earth-world be compared to what lies within the utterly clear and utterly void? Thus we know that heaven is only qi, the sun only fire, and the earth only water and soil. The myriad things are the dregs of qi, the moulding of fire, the warts of the earth. If one of the three is missing, creation is not completed. What more is there to doubt?”

paragraphs.orig: 虛子曰。人物之生。胎卵根子。各有其本。何待於日火乎。實翁曰。人物之生動。本於日火。使一朝無日。冷界凌兢。萬品融消。胎卵根子。將安所本。故曰地者萬物之母。日者萬物之父。天者萬物之祖也。

paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “Humans and things are born from womb, egg, root or seed, each with its own origin. Why wait on the sun’s fire?” Sirong said, “The birth and movement of humans and things are rooted in the sun’s fire. If suddenly there were no sun, the cold world would freeze and shiver, and the myriad kinds would melt away; womb, egg, root and seed, whence would they come? Therefore it is said: the earth is the mother of the myriad things, the sun is their father, and heaven is their ancestor.”

paragraphs.orig: 虛子曰。古云天不滿西北。地不滿東南。天地果有不滿歟。實翁曰。此中國之野言也。見北極之低旋。則疑天之不滿。見江河之東注。則疑地之不滿。泥於地勢之適然。不察環面之異觀。不亦愚乎。

paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “The ancients said that heaven is not full in the northwest and earth is not full in the southeast. Do heaven and earth truly have incompleteness?” Sirong said, “This is a rustic saying of China. Seeing the low circling of the northern pole, they suspect that heaven is incomplete; seeing the rivers flow eastward, they suspect that earth is incomplete. They are bogged down in the accidental configuration of the land and do not see the different aspects of the globe’s surface. Is that not foolish?”

paragraphs.orig: 虛子曰。地面之晝夜長短。彼此齊同。無有差別乎。實翁曰。豈其然乎。假如晝午於此。則自此以東九十度爲夕照。過此則爲昏曚。自此而西九十度爲朝暾。過此則爲晨曚。東西各一百八十度。卽此之對面而爲夜半。赤道南北各二十餘度。終年晝夜俱均。所差不過刻分。過此則晝夜之差漸多。極長或過十一時。極短或不及一時。至于兩極而赤道爲地平。則日在赤道上爲晝而占半年。日在赤道下爲夜。亦占半年。

paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “Are the lengths of day and night on the earth’s surface the same everywhere, without difference?” Sirong said, “How could that be? Suppose it is noon here. Then ninety degrees east of here is the evening glow, and beyond that is dusk; ninety degrees west of here is the morning sun, and beyond that is dawn twilight. East and west each extend one hundred and eighty degrees; the opposite side of this place is midnight. Twenty-odd degrees north and south of the equator, day and night are equal all year, the difference being no more than a few quarter-hours and minutes. Beyond this, the difference between day and night gradually increases; the longest may exceed eleven double-hours, and the shortest may fall short of one. At the two poles, where the equator becomes the horizon, when the sun is above the equator it is day and occupies half a year; when the sun is below the equator it is night and likewise occupies half a year.”

paragraphs.orig: 虛子曰。今夫海之爲物也。旱不渴雨不溢寒不氷。百川灌注而不變其鹹。朝汐隨時而不失其期。願聞其理。

paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “Now the sea: in drought it does not dry up, in rain it does not overflow, in cold it does not freeze; a hundred rivers pour into it and it does not change its saltiness; the morning tide follows the hour and never misses its time. I wish to hear the reason.”

paragraphs.orig: 實翁曰。月者水精也。水遇月則感而應之。湧而成浪。月有常道。潮有常期。浪勢簸掀。自成進退。近於本浪者。進退俱猛。遠於本浪者進退俱微。其益遠者。浪勢不及。不成潮汐也。海水雖大畜而不洩。近於赤道。日火蒸炙。轉成鹹味。味鹹如鹽豉。浪湧如灘水。地且近日。冬不成氷。若兩極之下。地候極冷。日火煮微而潮浪不及。則亦有氷海。且積水巨涵。汪洋無際。江海之灌。霖雨之浸。實如一杯之水。無所增損於千頃之陂。且江河之源。本於重泉。重泉之源。本於海水。水隨土脉。如激如吸。橫流倒行。無遠不到。土氣滲潤。變鹹爲淡。溢爲井泉。湊成江河。此是互相輸瀉。均是海水。且風陽之熯曝。人物之沃飮。足以當雨雪之淋漓。則不渴不溢。其勢然也。
