paragraphs.en: Sirong said, “The moon is the essence of water. Water meeting the moon feels and responds, surging into waves. The moon has a constant course and the tide a constant time; the waves heave and toss and of themselves make advance and retreat. Those near the source wave advance and retreat both fiercely; those far from the source wave advance and retreat both feebly; farther still, the wave’s force does not reach, and no tide is formed. Though the sea water is vast, it stores and does not leak. Near the equator, the sun’s fire steams and bakes it, and it turns salty; the taste is salty as salt or fermented beans, and the waves surge like shoal water. The land too is near the sun, and in winter no ice forms. At the two poles, where the climate is extremely cold, the sun’s fire cooks only faintly and the tidal waves do not reach, and so there are also icy seas. Moreover, the accumulated water is vast and boundless; the pouring in of rivers and the soaking of long rains are truly like a cup of water that adds or subtracts nothing from a pond of a thousand qing. Moreover, the sources of rivers lie in layered springs, and the source of the layered springs is sea water. The water follows the veins of the soil, as if stirred, as if sucked, flowing sideways and backwards, reaching every distance; the soil’s qi seeps and moistens, changing salt to fresh, overflowing as wells and springs and converging into rivers. Thus they pour into one another; all are sea water. Moreover, the drying of wind and sun, and the drinking and watering of humans and things, are enough to match the downpour of rain and snow; so it neither dries up nor overflows. Such is its force.”

paragraphs.orig: 虛子曰。古云桑海之變。亦有其理乎。實翁曰。余觀地界。人壽不過百年。國史未傳實蹟。地水之變。漸而不驟。人不能覺也。蚌蛤之殼。水磨之石。或在高山。海傍之山。類多沙白。此其互相進退。其蹟甚著。且觀中國。遼野千里。乃是九河故道。漠外沙磧。乃是黃河故道。孟子不云乎。洪水橫流。汎濫於中國。夫流沙淤塞。水道漸高。不能不橫決也。黃河橫決。正當堯時。崇伯不察時運。爲中國遠慮。欲復其故道。陻之九年。績用不成。堤防一壞。九州懷襄。禹乃嗣興。鑿龍門順其勢而導之。以救其急而卒爲中國患。觀乎此。則桑海之互變。可知也。

paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “The ancients spoke of the change of mulberry fields into sea; does that too have a principle?” Sirong said, “I look at the earth-world: human life does not exceed a hundred years, and national histories do not transmit the actual traces. The changes of earth and water are gradual, not sudden, and people cannot perceive them. Clam shells and water-worn stones are sometimes found on high mountains; mountains by the sea are mostly white with sand. These show their mutual advancing and retreating, and their traces are very clear. Look also at China: the plain of Liaoye, a thousand li across, is the old course of the Nine Rivers; the sandy waste beyond the desert is the old course of the Yellow River. Did Mencius not say that the floodwaters flowed everywhere and inundated the Middle Kingdom? When drifting sand silts up and the water channel gradually rises, it cannot but burst out sideways. The Yellow River’s bursting its banks took place precisely in the time of Yao. The Lord of Chong, not perceiving the tide of events and planning far ahead for China, wished to restore its old course; he dammed it for nine years, but his work was not accomplished. Once the embankments failed, the nine provinces were engulfed. Yu then took up the work, cut through Longmen, followed its natural force and guided it, relieving the urgency; yet in the end it became a plague for China. Observing this, one can know the mutual change of mulberry field and sea.”

paragraphs.orig: 虛子曰。地之有震。山之有遷。何也。實翁曰。地者活物也。脉絡榮衛。實同人身。特其體大持重。不如人身之跳動。是以少有變。則人必恠之。妄測其灾祥也。其實水火風氣周行流注。閡而成震。激而推遷。其勢然也。

paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “That the earth has quakes and mountains shift: why?” Sirong said, “The earth is a living thing. Its veins and vessels, its circulation of nourishing and guarding qi, are truly the same as the human body. It is simply that its body is large and steady, not leaping and pulsing as a human body does. So when there is a small change, people find it strange and rashly speculate on its omens of good or ill. In fact water, fire, wind and qi circulate, flowing and pouring; when blocked they cause quakes, and when stirred they push and shift. Such is their force.”

paragraphs.orig: 虛子曰。地之有溫泉鹽井。何也。實翁曰。太虛者。水之精也。太陽者。火之精也。地界者。水火之査滓也。地非水火。不能生活。旋轉定位。化成萬物。水火之力也。夫溫泉鹽井。水火之相盪也。

paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “Why does the earth have hot springs and salt wells?” Sirong said, “The Great Void is the essence of water; the Great Sun is the essence of fire; the earth-world is the dregs of water and fire. Without water and fire the earth could not live. Its rotating, its fixing of positions, its transforming and completing the myriad things are the power of water and fire. Hot springs and salt wells are water and fire stirring against each other.”

paragraphs.orig: ## 7. 장례와 풍수
paragraphs.en: 7. Burial and Geomancy

paragraphs.orig: 虛子曰。然則人之死也。葬不得其地。則風火之爲灾。亦有其理歟。
paragraphs.reading: 허자왈. 연칙인지사야. 장부득기지. 칙풍화지위재. 역유기리여.
paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “Then, when a person dies and is not buried in a proper place, is it also reasonable that wind and fire cause calamity?”

paragraphs.orig: 實翁曰。水火風氣。運行有脉。遇實則走。遇虛則集。葬失其道。灾必立至。翻覆焦坼。化生蟲廉。骨骸朽散。不得安厝。

paragraphs.en: Sirong said, “Water, fire, wind and qi circulate along veins; they run when they meet what is solid and gather when they meet what is empty. If burial misses its proper way, calamity comes at once: the corpse is overturned, scorched and cracked, and transforms into worms and roaches, the bones rot and scatter, and cannot rest in peace.”

paragraphs.orig: 虛子曰。方其葬人。土性凈潤。水火風蟲。無所形現。及其發開舊壙。絶少安吉。何也。

paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “At the time a person is buried, the soil is clean and moist, and water, fire, wind and worms show no form. Yet when the old grave is opened, rarely is it found safe and sound. Why?”

paragraphs.orig: 實翁曰。善哉問也。人之於父母。生則致其養。死則致其敬。遺書遺服。尊奉而謹藏之。敬之至也。况於遺骸乎。宅兆者。遺骸之藏也。敢不敬謹也。雖然。布帛衣衾。養生之具也。棺槨旌翣。美觀之文也。入土則腐汚穢遺骸。惟務目下之美觀。不念畢竟之汚穢。可謂孝且智乎。况虛必引物。地之理也。旌翣之備而槨虛。衣衾之腐而棺虛。瀝靑灰石之堅而壙虛。水火蟲風。皆由於虛。哀哉。藏父母之遺骸。內被腐穢。外引風火。肢節焦散。不保其體。於人心其能恔乎。

paragraphs.en: Sirong said, “A good question. Toward one’s parents, one offers nourishment in life and reverence in death. Even the books and clothes they left are venerated and carefully stored, which is the utmost reverence; how much more their remains! The grave is where the remains are stored; dare we not be reverent and careful? Even so, silks, cloths, shrouds and coverlets are tools for nourishing life; coffin, outer coffin, banners and feather fans are ornaments for fine appearance. When buried they rot and defile the remains. To labour only for present fine appearance and give no thought to the eventual defilement: can that be called filial and wise? Moreover, emptiness necessarily draws things in; such is the principle of the earth. When the banners and fans are provided, the outer coffin is empty; when the shrouds and bedding rot, the coffin is empty; when the pitch, lime and stone are hard, the grave pit is empty. Water, fire, worms and wind all come through emptiness. Alas! One buries one’s parents’ remains, and inside they suffer rot and filth, while outside they draw wind and fire, their limbs and joints scorched and scattered, unable to preserve their form. Can the human heart find ease in this?

paragraphs.orig: 夫土者。物之母也而生之本也。文繡不足以擬其美。珠玉不足以擬其凈。惟人生血肉。濕處則病。服用采色。近地則汚。是以高堂重茵。遠土以爲貴。陶穴藉處。近土以爲賤。人習故常。遂忘其本。及其死也。衾冒襲斂。惟恐其不厚。棺槨灰石。惟恐其不堅。深憂永圖。惟遠土是謀。殊不知死生異道。貴賤殊物。黃中溫潤。莫貴於土。眞美眞淨。實爲遺骸之寶藏也。是以不封不樹。太古之已愨也。包布裸葬。達士之弔詭也。茶毗舍利。佛氏之淨法也。堲周瓦棺。聖人之中制也。

paragraphs.en: “Earth is the mother of things and the root of life. Embroidery cannot match its beauty, and pearls and jade cannot match its purity. Human living flesh and blood fall ill in damp places; clothing and colours are soiled near the ground. Hence lofty halls and heavy mats, far from the soil, are deemed noble, and dug-out caves and mat-seats, near the soil, are deemed base. People are used to the ordinary and so forget the root. When they die, the wrapping, covering, dressing and shrouding are feared not to be thick enough; coffin, outer coffin, lime and stone are feared not to be strong enough. With deep concern and long planning, they seek only to be far from the soil. They do not realise that life and death take different ways and that noble and base differ in kind. The yellow centre, warm and moist: nothing is more precious than the soil. Truly beautiful and truly pure, it is in fact the treasure-store for the remains. Therefore to have neither mound nor trees was the sincerity of remote antiquity; wrapping in cloth and burying naked was the paradoxical reasoning of enlightened men; cremation with relics is the pure method of the Buddhists; the brick-lined and tile coffin was the sages’ middle-way institution.”

paragraphs.orig: 虛子曰。然則太上茶毗。其次裸葬。安用封樹堲瓦爲哉。實翁曰。葬師主義。葬親主恩。西竺之敎。割恩而立義。中國之敎。屈義而伸恩。王孫裸葬。矯俗之激也。生于中國。自有其義。崇其儉節其文。不忘其本。參以時義。勿循俗習。永思安厝。夫平原高崗。俱是福地。何有於風火之灾。此爲人子之所當知也。盖成周尙文。禮物太備。孟氏距墨。力排薄葬。重棺明器之具。無土親膚之論。不能無流弊也。

paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “Then cremation is best, naked burial next. Why use mounds, trees, brick lining and tile?” Sirong said, “The funeral master puts duty first; the burial of one’s parents puts affection first. The teaching of India cuts off affection and establishes duty; the teaching of China bends duty and extends affection. Yang Wangsun’s naked burial was a vehement correction of the custom. Born in China, one has one’s own duty here: honour its frugality and moderate its ornament; do not forget the root; take into account the demands of the times; do not follow vulgar habits; and long ponder a secure resting place. Plains and high ridges are all blessed sites; what room is there for calamity of wind and fire? This is what children ought to know. Now the Zhou were fond of ornament, and their ritual objects were over-elaborate; Mencius, resisting Mo Zi, strenuously rejected simple burial, and the preparation of double coffins and spirit articles and the argument against letting the soil touch the skin could not but have bad consequences.”

paragraphs.orig: 虛子曰。宅兆有吉凶。子姓有禍福。一氣感應。亦有其理乎。實翁曰。重囚在獄。宛轉楚毒。至不堪也。未聞重囚之子身發惡疾。况於死者之體魄乎。雖然。技術之妄。實無其理。傳信之久。衆心合靈。想無成有。往往有中人之機巧。天亦隨之。鑠金銷骨。自有其理。夫天文之祥祲。卜筮之休咎。禱祀之格響。地術之禍福。其理一也。蔡季通之得罪也。悔遷人墓。夫無故改葬。宜其罪悔。惟崇信左術。實爲罪悔之本。况紫陽之山陵議狀。專主術說。甚矣臺史。言出儒宗。人不敢議。異說鴟張。天下若狂。訟獄繁興。人心日壞。流弊之酷。奚啻頓悟事功之比而已哉。

paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “The grave site has good and ill fortune, and descendants have calamity or blessing; the response of a single qi: is there a principle in this too?” Sirong said, “A heavy prisoner in jail writhes in bitter torment, utterly unbearable. Yet I have never heard that the son of such a prisoner developed a malignant disease himself. How much less the bodies and souls of the dead? Even so, the falsity of the technique truly has no principle; but when something has long been handed down and trusted, the many hearts join their spirit; thought makes the nonexistent exist, and often hits upon the springs of people’s affairs, and Heaven too follows along. ‘Melting metal and dissolving bones’ has its own principle. The omens of astronomy, the good and ill of divination, the arrival and enjoyment of prayers and sacrifices, the fortune and calamity of geomancy: their principle is one. When Cai Jitong fell into guilt, he repented of having moved a person’s tomb. To rebury without cause deserves guilt and regret; but it was his reverence and belief in the heterodox art that was the root of the guilt and regret. Moreover, Zhu Xi’s memorial on the imperial tombs wholly upheld the art’s theories. How extreme! The pronouncements of the censor-historians came from the patriarch of the Confucians, and people dared not discuss them; heterodox theories spread like owls spreading their wings; the world seemed mad; lawsuits flourished, and human hearts grew worse by the day. The cruelty of the resulting evils goes far beyond even those of ‘sudden enlightenment’ and ‘practical merit.’”

paragraphs.orig: ## 8. 인류와 문명의 역사, 화이의 구분
paragraphs.en: 8. The History of Humankind and Civilisation, and the Chinese–Barbarian Distinction

paragraphs.orig: 虛子曰。天地之體形情狀。旣聞命矣。請卒聞人物之本。古今之變。華夷之分。
paragraphs.reading: 허자왈. 천지지체형정상. 기문명의. 청졸문인물지본. 고금지변. 화이지분.
paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “I have now heard the bodily form and conditions of heaven and earth. I ask finally to hear of the origin of humans and things, the changes from past to present, and the division between Chinese and barbarian.”

paragraphs.orig: 實翁曰。夫地者虛界之活物也。土者其膚肉也。水者其精血也。兩露者其涕汗也。風火者其魂魄榮衛也。是以水土釀於內。日火熏於外。元氣湊集。滋生衆物。草木者地之毛髮也。人獸者地之蚤蝨也。巖洞土窟。氣聚成質。謂之氣化。男女相感。形交胎產。謂之形化。邃古之時。專於氣化。人物不繁。鍾禀深厚。神智淸明。動止純厖。養生不資於物。喜怒不萌於心。呼吸吐納。不飢不渴。無營無欲。遊戱于于。鳥獸魚鼈。咸遂其生。草木金石。各葆其體。天無淫沴之灾。地無崩渴之害。此人物之本。眞太和之世也。

paragraphs.en: Sirong said, “The earth is a living creature of the empty realm. Soil is its flesh; water is its essence and blood; dew and rain are its tears and sweat; wind and fire are its soul-spirits and its nourishing and guarding qi. So water and soil ferment within and the sun’s fire heats from without; primordial qi gathers and breeds the multitude of things. Plants are the earth’s hair; humans and beasts are the earth’s fleas and lice. In cliff caves and earthen hollows, qi gathers and forms substance; this is called qi-transformation. Men and women feel each other, bodies unite, and there is gestation and birth; this is called form-transformation. In remotest antiquity there was only qi-transformation. Humans and things were not numerous, their endowment was deep and rich, their spirit and wisdom clear, their conduct pure and simple. They nourished life without depending on things; joy and anger did not sprout in their hearts; they breathed in and out and were neither hungry nor thirsty. Without scheming or desire, they roamed contentedly. Birds, beasts, fish and turtles all fulfilled their lives; plants, metals and stones each preserved their forms. Heaven had no calamity of excess and ill omen; earth had no harm of collapse or drying up. This was the origin of humans and things, truly an age of supreme harmony.”

paragraphs.orig: 降自中古。地氣始衰。人物生成。轉就駁濁。男女相聚。乃生情欲。感精結胎。始有形化。自有形化。人物繁衍。地氣益泄而氣化絶矣。氣化絶則人物之生。專禀精血。滓穢漸長。淸明漸退。此天地之否運。禍亂之權輿也。男女形交。精血耗竭。機巧攻心。神火焦熬。內有飢渴之患。外有寒暑之苦。囓草飮水。以充飢渴。巢居穴處。以御寒暑。於是萬物各私其身而民始爭矣。草水之薄而濫以佃漁。鳥獸魚鼈。不得遂其生矣。巢穴之陋而侈以棟宇。草木金石。不得葆其體矣。膏粱適其口而臟腑脆矣。布帛暖其體而支節解矣。園囿臺榭陂塘之役作而地力損矣。忿怒怨詛淫穢之氣昇而天灾現矣。

paragraphs.en: “From middle antiquity on, the earth’s qi began to decline. Humans and things came to be born more and more mottled and turbid. Men and women gathered together, and thereupon emotions and desires arose; essence was moved and the embryo conceived, and form-transformation began. Since form-transformation began, humans and things multiplied, the earth’s qi leaked further, and qi-transformation ceased. When qi-transformation ceased, the birth of humans and things came to rely entirely on essence and blood, and dregs and filth gradually increased while clarity and brightness gradually receded. This is the age of obstruction of heaven and earth, the beginning of calamity and disorder. When male and female unite in body, essence and blood are exhausted, cunning attacks the heart, and the fire of the spirit is scorched. Within there is the affliction of hunger and thirst; without there is the suffering of cold and heat. They gnawed grass and drank water to fill their hunger and thirst, and lived in nests and caves to guard against cold and heat. Thereupon each of the myriad things began to be selfish about its own body, and the people began to contend. Where grass and water were scanty they hunted and fished excessively, and birds, beasts, fish and turtles could not fulfil their lives. Where nests and caves were crude they extravagantly built halls and houses, and plants, metals and stones could not preserve their forms. Rich food suited their mouths and their viscera grew fragile; cloth and silk warmed their bodies and their limbs slackened. The labour of gardens, parks, terraces, pavilions, embankments and ponds was set going and the earth’s strength was damaged; the qi of anger, resentment, cursing and lewd filth rose and heavenly calamities appeared.

paragraphs.orig: 於是勇智多欲者生於其間。驅率同心。各占雄長。弱者服其勞。强者享其利。割裂疆界。睢盱兼幷。治兵格鬪。張拳肉薄。民始傷其生矣。巧者運技。挑發殺氣。鍊金刳木。凶器作矣。刀戈之銳。弧矢之毒。爭城爭地。伏尸原野。盖生民之禍至此而極矣。

paragraphs.en: “Thereupon the courageous, clever and covetous arose among them, driving and leading followers of the same mind, each seizing leadership. The weak served in labour and the strong enjoyed the profits. They carved up borders, glared and annexed, drilled troops and fought, raised fists and came to grips. The people began to harm their lives. The cunning plied their skill, provoked the spirit of killing, smelted metals and hollowed out wood, and weapons of ill omen were made: the sharpness of blades and halberds, the poison of bows and arrows. They fought for cities and for land, and corpses lay on the plains. The calamity of the people’s lives reached its extreme here.

paragraphs.orig: 冀方千里。號稱中國。負山臨海。風水渾厚。日月淸照。寒暑適宜。河嶽鍾靈。篤生善良。夫伏羲神農黃帝堯舜氏作而茅茨土階。身先儉德。以制民產。欽文恭讓。躬行明德。以敷民彜。文敎洋溢。天下煕皥。此中國所謂聖人之功化至治之世也。

paragraphs.en: “The region of Ji, a thousand li in extent, is called the Middle Kingdom. It has mountains at its back and the sea before it; its geomantic energy is deep and generous, the sun and moon shine clearly, cold and heat are fitting, and the rivers and peaks gather spirit and bring forth the good and gentle. Then the lords Fu Xi, Shen Nong, the Yellow Emperor, Yao and Shun arose; they lived in thatched huts with earthen steps, putting frugal virtue first in their own persons, and thereby regulated the people’s livelihood; they honoured culture and practised courtesy, themselves performing bright virtue, and thereby spread the people’s constant norms. Culture and teaching overflowed and the world was in joyous peace. This is what China calls the age of the sages’ meritorious transformation and supreme order.

paragraphs.en: “To follow the times and accord with custom is the sages’ expedient, the art of regulating government. As for supreme harmony and pure simplicity, it is not that the sages did not desire them; but as times shifted and customs formed, prohibitions and defences no longer worked, and to oppose and suppress them made the disorder grow worse, so that the sages’ strength truly could not suffice. Hence it is said, ‘Living in the present age and wishing to return to the ways of the past, calamity will reach one’s person.’ Since the feelings of desire cannot be forbidden, they instituted the rites of marriage, fixing husband and wife as pairs, merely forbidding licentiousness. Since dwellings cannot be forbidden, they let there be thatched huts with roofs of tangled weeds, unpolished and unhewn, merely forbidding ostentation. Since the eating of fish and meat cannot be forbidden, they had angling without netting and strictly regulated the mountains and marshes, merely forbidding excess. Since clothing of cloth and silk cannot be forbidden, they made different regulations for old and young and gave distinctions to high and low, merely forbidding extravagance. Thus rites, music, institutions and regulations were how the sages patched leaks and mended gaps, restraining for a time by expedient; but the roots of feeling were not pulled out nor the sources of profit stopped. The force was like damming a river, which in the end bursts. The sages already knew this.

paragraphs.en: “The ruler of Xia handed the throne to his son, and the people began to treat their households as private; Tang and Wu banished and killed their rulers, and the people began to offend their superiors. This was not the fault of those few lords. It was the remainder of the age of supreme order and the gradual onset of decline and disorder; the trend of the times was so. Xia valued loyalty and Shang valued simplicity, but compared with Tang and Yu they were already more ornamented. The institutions of Zhou were devoted wholly to ostentation and show. From the time of Kings Zhao and Mu, the sovereign’s authority had already decayed; government lay with the many marquises, and the king merely held an empty vessel, living parasitically above them. Without waiting for the injuries of Kings You and Li, the world had long been without a Zhou.

paragraphs.en: “Moreover, to discard Weizi and Jizi and install Wugeng meant that the Way of Yin was not restored; the subtle intent behind raising up Zhou can hardly be concealed. When King Cheng first took the throne, Guan and Cai quarrelled within the walls; the eastern campaign lasted three years, and the axe was notched and the hatchet broken; eight proclamations were issued to the land of Mei, and the stubborn people resisted transformation. Could Zhou’s replacing of Yin have been without a heart for profit in the world? Confucius praised Shun, calling him a sage by virtue; but of King Wu he said only that he ‘did not lose his fine reputation in the world.’ He praised Taibo for ‘supreme virtue,’ but of Wu’s music he said that it was ‘not perfectly good.’ Confucius’s meaning can be clearly seen.

paragraphs.en: “From the Zhou onward, the royal way declined day by day and the arts of hegemony ran rampant: those who feigned benevolence became emperors; those with strong troops became kings; those who used cunning were honoured; those good at flattery flourished. A ruler governed his ministers by feeding them favour and salary; a minister served his ruler by luring him with power and scheming. With half-faces of tallies matched, with a single eye guarding against misfortune, above and below pulling in pincers, together they accomplished their private ends. Alas, how wretched! The teeming multitudes of the world met one another harbouring profit. Economising expenses and remitting taxes was not for the sake of the people; honouring the worthy and employing the able was not for the sake of the state; punishing rebels and attacking the guilty was not to forbid violence; giving generously and receiving sparingly, and not treasuring distant goods, was not to cherish the distant. They only preserved the inheritance and guarded their positions, honoured and glorious until death, handing it down for two or three generations, endlessly. This is what is called the accomplished work of a worthy ruler and the fine counsel of a loyal minister.

paragraphs.orig: 或曰。木石之灾。肇於有巢。鳥獸之禍。創於包羲。飢饉之憂。由於燧人。巧僞之智。華靡之習。本於蒼頡。縫掖之偉容。不如左袵之便易。揖讓之虛禮。不如膜拜之眞率。文章之空言。不如騎射之實用。暖衣火食。體骨脆軟。不如毳幕潼酪。筋脉勁悍。此或是過甚之論。而中國之不振則所由來者漸矣。混沌鑿而大樸散。文治勝而武力衰。處士橫議。周道日蹙。秦皇焚書。漢業少康。石渠分爭。新莽簒位。鄭馬演經。三國分裂。晉氏淸談。神州陸沈。六朝附庸於江左。五胡跳盪於宛洛。拓跋正位於北朝。西凉一統於唐祚。遼金迭主。合於松漠。朱氏失統。天下薙髮。夫南風之不競。胡運之日長。乃人事之感召。天時之必然也。

paragraphs.en: “Some say: the calamity of wood and stone began with Youchao; the misfortune of birds and beasts started with Baoxi; the worry of famine came from Suiren; cunning and falsity of wisdom and the habit of ornate extravagance have their root in Cang Jie. The grand bearing of wide-sleeved robes is not as convenient and easy as left-fastened lapels; the empty ritual of bowing and yielding is not as genuine and frank as prostration; the empty words of literary composition are not as practically useful as horse-riding and archery. Dressed warmly and eating cooked food, the body and bones become brittle and soft, unlike those who live in felt tents and drink curds, whose sinews and veins are strong and fierce. This may be an extreme argument, but that China is not vigorous has come about gradually from such causes. Chaos was bored with orifices and the great uncarved simplicity was scattered; civil government prevailed and martial strength declined. Retired scholars debated at will and the Way of Zhou shrank day by day. Qin burned the books; the Han enterprise enjoyed a modest peace; at Shiqu there were contending factions; Wang Mang usurped the throne; Zheng and Ma elaborated the Classics; the Three Kingdoms split apart; the Jin clique indulged in pure talk and the Divine Land sank on dry land; the Six Dynasties were vassals of Jiangzuo, the Five Barbarians leapt and raged over Wan and Luo; the Tuoba took the throne in the northern court; Western Liang was unified under the Tang line; Liao and Jin successively ruled and united at Songmo; the house of Zhu lost the succession, and the whole world shaved its heads. That the southern wind is not vigorous and the barbarian fortune grows daily longer is a summoning by human affairs and a necessity of heaven’s timing.”

paragraphs.en: Heoja said, “Confucius wrote the Spring and Autumn Annals, treating China as inner and the four barbarians as outer. Thus the distinction between Chinese and barbarian is this strict. Now you, Master, attribute it to a summoning by human affairs and a necessity of heaven’s timing. Is that not unacceptable?”

paragraphs.orig: 實翁曰。天之所生。地之所養。凡有血氣。均是人也。出類拔華。制治一方。均是君王也。重門深濠。謹守封疆。均是邦國也。章甫委貌。文身雕題。均是習俗也。自天視之。豈有內外之分哉。是以各親其人。各尊其君。各守其國。各安其俗。華夷一也。夫天地變而人物繁。人物繁而物我形。物我形而內外分。臟腑之於肢節。一身之內外也。四體之於妻子。一室之內外也。兄弟之於宗黨。一門之內外也。鄰里之於四境。一國之內外也。同軌之於化外。天地之內外也。夫非其有而取之謂之盜。非其罪而殺之謂之賊。四夷侵疆。中國謂之寇。中國瀆武。四夷謂之賊。相寇相賊。其義一也。孔子周人也。王室日卑。諸侯衰弱。吳楚滑夏。寇賊無厭。春秋者周書也。內外之嚴。不亦宜乎。雖然。使孔子浮于海。居九夷。用夏變夷。興周道於域外。則內外之分。尊攘之義。自當有域外春秋。此孔子之所以爲聖人也。

paragraphs.en: Sirong said, “What heaven gives birth to and earth nourishes, all that have blood and breath, are equally human. Those who stand out above their kind and govern a region are equally rulers. Those with double gates and deep moats who carefully guard their borders are equally states. The Zhangfu and Weimao caps, tattooed bodies and carved foreheads are equally customs. Seen from heaven, how could there be an inside and an outside? Hence each cherishes its own people, honours its own ruler, guards its own state, and is at ease in its own customs; Chinese and barbarians are one. When heaven and earth changed, humans and things multiplied; when humans and things multiplied, self and other took shape; when self and other took shape, inside and outside were divided. The viscera to the limbs is the inside and outside of one body; the four limbs to wife and children is the inside and outside of one household; brothers to clansmen is the inside and outside of one family; neighbours to the four borders is the inside and outside of one state; those within the same cart-gauge to those beyond civilisation is the inside and outside of heaven and earth. To take what is not one’s own is called robbery; to kill one who has no guilt is called brigandage. When the four barbarians invade the borders, China calls them raiders; when China abuses military force, the four barbarians call it brigandage. Raiding and brigandage are the same in meaning. Confucius was a man of Zhou. The royal house dwindled day by day, the lords were weak, Wu and Chu disordered Xia, and robbers and brigands were insatiable. The Spring and Autumn is a Zhou book; the strictness of inside and outside is surely fitting. Even so, had Confucius floated over the sea and dwelt among the Nine Yi, used Xia to change the Yi, and raised the Way of Zhou beyond the borders, then the distinction of inside and outside and the principle of honouring the king and repelling the barbarians would naturally have given an Overseas Spring and Autumn. This is why Confucius was a sage.”
